Portuguese soccer star Quévin Castro died at age 25 on August 22 after collapsing during a preseason match between his team, Real Sport Clube, and rivals Estrela de Amadora at Estádio das Seixas in Malveira, Portugal. In Real Sport Clube’s tribute to Castro, the team remembered him as “far more than a player.” (Castro signed with the club in June and never got to play in an official match for them.) “He was a member of our family, leaving a mark on all those who had the privilege of knowing him, both on and off the pitch,” Real Sport Clube’s statement read. Castro’s former team West Bromwich Albion announced plans to pay tribute to him during the following day’s match. “West Bromwich Albion are devastated to learn of the untimely passing of Quevin Castro, aged just 25. Albion will pay tribute to Quevin on Sunday, with a period of applause in the 25th minute of the fixture against Burnley. [Coach] James Morrison’s men will also wear black armbands,” the team confirmed.

News broke on August 16 that New York Yankees icon Tommy John died at age 83 after battling bladder cancer. The Challenge alum Tyler Duckworth’s mother, Joni, announced on August 13 that her son had died at age 44 earlier in the week. No cause of death has been determined as of publication. Duckworth was a pioneer for LGBTQ+ contestants on The Challenge as a two-time winner of the Cutthroat and Rivals seasons. Many Challenge cast members paid tribute to the late reality star following the announcement of his death. “Absolutely heartbroken to hear about Tyler. We shared something special being part of The Challenge family,” Brad Fiorenza wrote via Instagram. “I’ll always be grateful for the memories we shared; especially at this last event just a couple weeks ago. Tyler will be deeply missed by so many. May his amazing soul live on in the lives he’s touched. RIP my dear friend 🕊️🙏” The Challenge star Tina Barta shared her own memorial message, writing, “Some friendships are measured in years. Others are measured in memories, laughter, shared experiences and the way someone makes you feel when they are in the room. @themightyduckworth you are one of those special people. A true friend and confidant.💔… Tyler, thank you for being part of my story. I’m grateful our paths crossed in this crazy life and that I get to carry those memories with me. Rest peacefully, my darling friend 🕊️.”

Reggie Bannister died at age 80 on August 9 at his cabin in Crestline, California, his wife Gigi confirmed to TMZ. Gigi revealed that Reggie had a myriad of health problems — including Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease— due to being exposed to the herbicide Agent Orange while serving in the U.S. military during the Vietnam War. He is best known for playing the shotgun-wielding hero Reggie in the Phantasm horror movies. Other notable credits include supporting parts in 1990’s Silent Night, Deadly Night 4: Initiation, 1997’s Wishmaster and Bruce Campbell’s 2002 cult classic Bubba Ho-Tep.

The South Carolina Senator’s spokesperson confirmed on July 11 that Lindsey Graham died at age 71 following “a brief and sudden illness.”

South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster said via X that he was “devastated” over Graham’s death.

“Lindsey Graham is irreplaceable,” McMaster wrote. “The fiercest of fighters for South Carolina and America — and a loyal and steadfast friend. We grieve with [Lindsey’s sister] Darline, his family and his devoted staff. May God hold him gently in the palm of his hand. We shall not see his likes again.”

Credit: Courtesy Instagram / Aqueelah Chloe Adendorf

The South African Football Players Union announced Mamelodi Sundowns and Bafana Bafana midfielder Jayden Adams' death on July 11, only a few weeks after he competed in the World Cup. No cause of death was immediately announced. “His passing is an immeasurable loss to his family, teammates, clubs, the football fraternity and the country at large,” the organization said in a statement. “Death has cruelly stolen one of our own. It has robbed our nation of a remarkable footballer, but it will never take away the legacy Jayden Adams leaves behind. We will forever remember his humanity, his extraordinary talent and the pride with which he represented South Africa.” “There are no words to describe the pain I’m feeling. 💔 “Rest in peace, my love,” Adams’ girlfriend Aqueelah Chloe Adendorf wrote via Instagram. “Thank you for every memory, every laugh, every hug, and every moment we shared. You were not only the love of my life but also my greatest supporter and my best friend." She went on, “A part of my heart left with you, and I will carry your love with me forever. Until we meet again, I’ll miss you every single day. Rest easy, my angel. I love you always and forever." FIFA president Gianni Infantino added in his own statement, “It is so incredibly sad to hear that South Africa midfielder Jayden Adams has passed away just weeks after featuring in his nation’s historic FIFA World Cup campaign. My thoughts and condolences, as well as those of everyone at FIFA and the global football community, are with his family, friends and teammates. The Bafana and Mamelodi Sundowns star will be sorely missed. May he rest in peace.”

#3733. Sam Rockwell Breaks Down Scenes From His Career, Including ‘Charlie’s Angels’ and ‘The White Lotus’

“Thank God for Marvin Gaye and this song,” Sam Rockwell says while watching a younger version of himself dance opposite a stunned Drew Barrymore in the 2000 action-comedy Charlie’s Angels. “I mean, this song really makes the scene.”

While telling stories from his more than 35-year career across film and television for Vanity Fair’s Scene Selection, Rockwell says people tried to stop him from appearing in the remake of the 1970s TV series starring Barrymore, Cameron Diaz, and Lucy Liu. When he joined the project as secretly evil software engineer Eric Knox—who starts the film as Barrymore’s love interest—the script was “a work in progress,” Rockwell recalls. “A lot of people told me not to do this movie. And then, they all ate their words. It had a very specific kind of popcorn vibe to it, very unique, and I don’t think I’ve seen [it] since.”

Rockwell originally envisioned a more “punk rock” direction for his character, but changed his approach after speaking with friend and former Galaxy Quest costar Alan Rickman. “You know, Sam, keep it simple,” Rockwell recalled the late actor telling him. “When I did Die Hard, I killed someone and ate a sandwich.”

Over the decades, Rockwell tried his hand at a mix of projects—somber indies like sci-fi drama Moon (2009), studio awards contenders including The Green Mile (1999), and mainstream fare like Iron Man 2 (2010). “I was dating Leslie Bibb when Iron Man one came out…. It sort of changed superhero movies,” says Rockwell, whose now real-life partner of nearly 20 years appeared in the first film.

After being cast in the sequel as fast-talking arms dealer Justin Hammer, Rockwell learned that he would share most of his scenes with Mickey Rourke as fellow fictional baddie and Russian physicist Ivan Vanko. “Mickey didn’t want to meet me until we were on camera,” Rockwell remembers. “It was a wild experience…. Because my scenes were dialogue-driven, whereas a lot of [the rest of] it was special effects…it was a surprisingly actor-friendly experience being that it was a studio movie for me.”

Bibb and Rockwell, who also shared scenes in Iron Man 2, reunited onscreen in 2025 for season three of The White Lotus as it was filmed in Thailand. He joined the series partway through production, tasked with performing Mike White’s “brilliant monologue” about sex addiction and gender identity opposite Walton Goggins. “Leslie helped me get off-book in South Africa; we were on safari,” says Rockwell, who says he based his searching Buddhist character, Frank, on Martin Sheen in Apocalypse Now.

The actor also detailed the past screen inspiration behind his Oscar-winning performance in Martin McDonagh’s drama, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri (2017), calling the trajectory of his role as a bigoted local cop, “[The Andy Griffith Show’s] Barney Fife becomes [Taxi Driver’s] Travis Bickle,” says Rockwell. He joins forces with McDonagh once more for the new awards-season contender Wild Horse Nine, in which he acts with teenage idol John Malkovich. “I love characters who change and are underestimated by the audience,” says Rockwell of Three Billboards. “And this is really that.”

#3731. Nintendo Switch Players Will Soon Be Able To Gift Digital Games, Kinda

A new Switch system update later this month is finally bringing us the ability to gift games via the Nintendo eShop, albeit with some hefty restrictions.

Digital games are increasingly becoming the norm across the games industry, yet strangely the concept of gifting digital games has yet to be widely adopted across all storefronts. While Steam and many PC platforms have supported the ability to send digital games to friends for at least a decade, on console only Microsoft allows Xbox players to do the same. Without it, people have simply had to make do with digital store cards. For Nintendo platforms, however, the company are promising to slightly change that and allow directly gifting games, âjust in time for the holidays.â

The feature, added in firmware update 23.5.0 and launching November 16, will allow players within a family group on Nintendo Switch to gift digital games to one another via the eShop. Once the feature has been activated, players will need to navigate to a gameâs store page where a check box will allow us to give the game as a gift. After checkout, you’ll select the player within your “family” to give the game, select from eight colors of digital wrapping paper, and the game will appear on their system.

There are notable limitations to this new feature. Supervised accounts within a family group are unable to gift games, and the number of games able to be purchased and gifted within an unspecified period is limited. Some games may also be unavailable for gifting, and any games gifted are immediately sent to the receiving player (so donât go buying those Christmas gifts early!). The feature, however, will be available to players both on the original Nintendo Switch as well as the Switch 2.

Itâs a welcome addition, though the inability to freely gift a game to anyone on your friends list (as seen on Steam) makes the feature bizarrely limited. Still, the fact its available at all is welcome for parents of gaming kids, or the found family of friends sharing a Nintendo Switch Online Family Plan.

Presley Gerber tragically passed away after working toward addiction recovery in September of this year. He left behind his famous parents, Cindy Crawford and Casamigos businessman Rande Gerber, and his sister Kaia, who have all been reeling in the wake of his death. This week, the Bottoms cast member addressed that grief head on with a viral post about grief “coming in waves.”

It’s from The Year of Magical Thinking by Joan Didion, a book with a lighthearted title that betrays its heavy subject material and that I still think about to this day. It helped me get through my mother’s battle with cancer, and I think it’s a helpful read for anyone going through it with a loved one. However, it particularly highlights grief in the face of addiction, and I would guess was especially pertinent to Gerber.

Kaia shared a post this week about the titles on grief that have been helpful after losing her brother. A separate slide included a quote from Didion that's one of the more memorable from the book.

Grief, when it comes, is nothing we expect it to be. Grief has no distance. Grief, comes in waves, paroxysms, sudden apprehensions that weaken the knees and blind the eyes and obliterate the dailiness of life.

Here's what else she's been reading in recent days, per her post.

A post shared by Library Science (@libraryscience)

Didion wrote The Year of Magical Thinking in 2005, while frequenting hospitals as her daughter Quintana Roo dealt with health issues. All of this came just shortly after losing her husband, beloved author John Gregory Dunne. The book follows Didion’s experience with grief following her husband’s death alongside her daughter’s hospitalizations and complications related to alcohol abuse. The book ends without us knowing what was next for Quintana Roo and Didion, though her daughter would pass away in August of 2005, just shortly before the author would publish the book.

Joan Didion mixes up stories about experiences she'd shared with her family over time with prose about everything she was also going through in the moment. It’s beautiful, direct, and devastating writing. I wouldn’t recommend picking it up as a beach read, but if you are going through something in your family, it’s helpful for contextualizing feelings and realizing humans are similar. We all go through the pain and anger and feelings of helplessness when we are losing a loved one.

It's not one of the author's titles that have yet made it to the big screen, but Didion’s book is powerful. I read almost 10 years ago and some of her words are still with me. It holds up years after it was published, and it’s a gripping read. I’m glad Kaia Gerber found solace in it. I hope her parents, and celebrity pals like George and Amal Clooney, have found some solace too.

#3729. The Curious Case of Olivia Reingold’s AI Photo at a Democratic Victory Party: Valentino, Chanel, and a Free Press Mystery

On Monday night, the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, the fashion crowd celebrated at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, colloquially referred to as the Oscars of American fashion. Tory Burch was honored with the Positive Change Award, which was presented to her by Anna Wintour, the global editorial director of Vogue and chief content officer of Condé Nast. In her remarks, Wintour made the evening’s only direct reference to the midterms, reminiscing about attending a fundraising event for James Talarico, who successfully flipped Texas in the race for the Senate last night, alongside Burch. After applause from the audience, Wintour, a prolific Democratic fundraiser herself, looked up and addressed the room: “Let’s hope all of Texas feels the way you do,” she said.

The American fashion crowd has largely distanced itself from politics since the 2024 election. During their time in the White House as first ladies, Michelle Obama and Jill Biden were staunch supporters of the American fashion industry, often wearing American designers for public appearances. Melania Trump, in contrast, has more often preferred European labels. It’s an MO that trickles down into the political parties they represent.

There were many headlines that came out of last night’s midterms: Talarico flipped Texas, Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina, New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia and Deb Haaland of New Mexico became the first Black and Native American women, respectively, to be elected governor in the history of the US.

And yet it wasn’t just good news (and many great memes) that circulated in my group chats last night; there were also some fashion choices worth noting. First, the most pressing: Where were Steve Kornacki’s khakis? And what was the reasoning behind Haley Stevens’s ludicrously capacious hat? Some questions in life simply go unanswered.

Kornacki, a national political correspondent for NBC News, does not make his political affiliations public. But men in his age range (he is 47) and in the generations that follow—millennials and Gen Z—have been contending with what formalwear means and signals today.

Democratic men have been hard at work on their public image since the 2024 election, largely distancing themselves from the MAGA look and its too-large suits and extra-wide ties. In separating themselves from the manosphere, men like Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Senate race in Michigan, and Jon Ossoff, who was reelected to the Senate in Georgia, have been dressing more like the less buttoned up, progressive men they represent and less like the old establishment politicians on both the right and the left.

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed often sported tees and sweaters rather than button-downs and ties, frequently wearing taut sweaters and henleys under his suit jacket, while Ossoff largely opted for rolled cuffs and no jacket. As the two delivered victory speeches last night, they each wore a tailored suit—a little too tight in the arms; these are men who seem to eat their fair share of protein—and ditched their tie.

It’s a familiar image of a more laid-back look, but one in stark contrast to that of the faces of the right: Donald Trump, JD Vance, et al. Ossoff and El-Sayed, similarly to Kamala Harris during her presidential bid, also leaned into what was happening on the internet. These days, netizens are happy to objectify men and christen a new internet boyfriend every week. Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s campaigns seemed to understand the power of thirst—that their suits were too tight was most likely not completely intentional, but it did help underscore a simple fact: that they are fit, and that their virility can be both attractive and nonthreatening all at once.

Zohran Mamdani speaking at an event on election night. Mamdani also ditched his tie on Tuesday, in line with some of his fellow Democrats.

It is worth noting, however, that there are some men further to the left, both in politics and around it, who have reembraced the suit: Zohran Mamdani and Hasan Piker. On one hand, this has served a similar purpose as Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s choices: It has distanced them from looksmaxxers and other conservative-leaning young men. On the other hand, a suit for Mamdani and Piker signifies what suits have always represented: that these are grown men doing important things.

The men are not the full story, however. Bottoms and Haaland came as they are, nodding to the communities they represent. The former wore a bright fuchsia suit and matching blouse, a callback to the lively and monochromatic dressing that is a deeply embedded and celebrated tradition in Black church culture. Haaland’s jewelry—firefly earrings and a beaded necklace—nodded at the style of accessories that is representative of Native style and fashion. If there is something that fashion clearly signifies, it’s community and belonging.

It is a running punch line that the left is more closely connected to fashion—it’s the wine-and-cheese crowd, the elites. (Hillary Clinton, during her bid for the presidency in 2016, was dragged online and by the press for wearing an Armani jacket that reportedly retailed for some $12,000 while delivering a speech that touched on income inequality.) While it’s true that fashion designers are often more enthusiastic about dressing progressives than they are about dressing conservatives, in the era of Trump and the MAGA look, this has become a half-baked story.

Olivia Reingold, a staff writer at The Free Press, made a post on X last night while reporting from an event for the Michigan Democratic Party. “So far at Abdul El-Sayed’s election night event I’ve spotted, Valentino heels, a Chanel bag, a Moncler jacket, Rolex watches, and a YSL bag among other designer items,” Reingold wrote, captioning an image of a woman holding a gold quilted Chanel handbag and a pair of Valentino Rockstud leather pumps.

Read Fit Check: Your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

When one takes a closer look, however, the image has several discrepancies. The style and make of the Chanel Flap bag is inconsistent with others the brand has sold, and the Valentino shoes in question appear askew in proportion; their straps have several punched holes that the authentic Valentino style does not. This could mean that the products in the image are not authentic, but there is another suggestive tell: The bottom strap on the left shoe appears to cut through its connecting strap rather than around, a classic mistake made when artificial intelligence is used to create or alter an image. A run of the image through several AI detectors, including SynthID, a digital watermarking approach created by Google DeepMind that detects media generated by OpenAI, Google, Nvidia, and Kakao, suggests the use of AI. SynthID detected that “this media was made or edited with OpenAI.” (Vanity Fair has reached out to Chanel and Valentino to advise on the authenticity of the products.)

Reingold did not reply to a request for comment, but on Thursday afternoon followed up with a new post on X, admitting to using AI “to brighten and sharpen an image of a woman in Valentino shoes and a Chanel bag.”

It’s become too easy to try to make a point about the left’s fashion choices: that Rama Duwaji, wife of Mamdani, should not wear pricey shoes, even if borrowed, because of her political beliefs; or that Democratic women should not carry Valentino or Chanel and vote for a candidate seeking to tax the wealthy. Therein lies the crux of the argument: Does this mean that luxury shoppers should align themselves with MAGA because it’s a party associated with billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos and logo-clad celebs like Nicki Minaj, who wore Chanel to the polls in New Hampshire? The answer is simple: no.

Our fashion choices say much about our values, identity, and aspirations. And while politicians have oftentimes utilized fashion to align themselves with specific groups or appear friendly to voters, they, in broad strokes, do not define our political affiliations. A Chanel bag does not make a Democrat, just as a red tie does not make a Republican.

#3728. Elizabeth Holmes' Partner Billy Evans Claims He Wrestled Nathan Fielder

Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, allegedly wrestled filmmaker Nathan Fielder in a deleted scene from the documentary You Can See Everything.

“I really wish they’d kept the scene where I wrestled Nathan, Borat style,” Evans, 34, wrote via X on Sunday, November 8, referencing a scene from Sacha Baron Cohen’s 2006 comedy Borat. “Full top mount. His little Canadian frame struggling beneath me.”

Evans added that he “thought [Fielder] was in on the joke, until he wasn’t.”

“Imagine realizing that [on] camera,” he continued. “This literally wouldn’t make the top 10 best deleted scenes. We didn’t hold back. We showed them everything. You saw what they wanted to show you …. It was a wild experience. Hate us, live [sic] us, the truth or lack there of is in the edit.”

Evans responded to several fans who asked for clarification on the alleged wrestling scene.

“Clothed,” he wrote when asked if he was “naked” while entangled with Fielder, 43, a reference to the scene in which Borat was nude as he wrestled his producer (played by Ken Davitian). “But [codirector] Lance Oppenheim asked him to 1) stand by the edge of the pool 2) remove his phone and monitor 3) look up. Then I tossed Nathan into the pool. Borat wrestling ensued. I thought it was a bit. It wasn’t.”

Evans also agreed with a fan who encouraged Fielder and Oppenheim, 30, to “release the footage” that wasn’t shown in the final edit of the A24-produced doc, which hit theaters on October 16.

“They filmed us for 3 years. Everything. Imagine your life for 3 years. Every conversation up for debate, with someone else deciding what to show,” he wrote. “But yes. I advocate for it.”

You Can See Everything pulls back the curtain on Holmes’ life in the month leading up to the start of her 11-year federal prison sentence in 2023. The meta doc — which turns the lens on itself to show the film crew and cameras at work — also features footage of Evans from 2025.

Holmes, 42, is the former CEO of Theranos, a company she founded in 2003 and claimed would create a revolutionary medical device that could run hundreds of complex health tests from a tiny pinprick of blood. An investigation in 2015 discovered that the technology did not work, and Holmes was accused of deceiving high-profile investors.

In January 2022, a jury found Holmes guilty of four counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. She was sentenced in November 2022 to 11 years and three months in federal prison and reported to a facility in Bryan, Texas, in May 2023. (Holmes was also ordered to pay 12 victims a total of $452 million in restitution. Her former business partner and ex, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, was sentenced to nearly 13 years in federal prison and ordered to pay a share of the $452 million to their victims.)

In September, Holmes secured an early release from the minimum-security Federal Prison Camp in Bryan and is scheduled to be transferred to a halfway house, the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, in August 2027 — three years before she was previously expected to be released from prison.

#3727. Valve Is Improving The Data About How Well A Game Will Run On Your Steam Deck

Steam has delivered a refresh of its store page for Steam Deck owners, allowing people to see the average framerate a game will run at on the handheld device based on the performance data of other players.

While games often arrive as verified to work on Steam Deck, this doesn’t always translate to workingÂ well. To let players know just how well a game will perform on Valve’s portable PC, others who have opted in to share their data will contribute to a consensus on possible framerates.

Under the additional info for Steam Deck compatibility on the game page, a new note will display the average framerate. It will also be possible to expand this data further by looking at the histogram, which will qualify the average into a graph that not only displays how common it is for a game to run at that framerate, but also how often the game hitches or stutters for players.

According to Valve, although the current information relies on standardized test criteria, the denominations âmay not match every customerâs bar for acceptable gameplay.â The company is also planning to expand this feature beyond Steam Deck in order to provide framerate information for more devices. The feature is already live for games with enough data points to provide an average. For example, right now Final Fantasy VII Rebirth shows that Steam Deck OLED players run the game at an average of 37 frames per second, while those playing Hades II are seeing 88 FPS on the same hardware.

With portable PC devices like Steam Deck, ROG Ally and even the Ayn Thor becoming more standard for players who donât need the most expensive hardware, seeing how a game will perform with more specificity is only a good thing. It doesnât hurt that Steam are planning to expand the Steam Deck lineup in future, and having such features available only makes the hardware more accessible for those less accustomed to PC gaming.

#3725. Russell Brand Has Been Found Guilty. American Courts Could Learn a Lot From His Trial

Britain’s most notorious serial killers and infamous gangsters are convicted at London’s Old Bailey, under a neo-Baroque dome and gold-gilded statue of Lady Justice. But it is Southwark Crown Court, an entirely bland heap of 1980s bricks by the River Thames, where the embattled entertainers wash up.

Only recently, this is where rapper Chris Brown—who pleaded guilty to affray after striking a man in the head with a glass bottle in a nightclub—learned he would avoid prison. It is also where Russell Brand today was found guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault. He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The week before, whilst reporting on Brand’s trial, I watched a fan in the corridor outside the courtroom admiringly accost the comedian. “I’ve been told to tell you there are many who support you,” she told him. He gave a zen reply: “I receive it, I receive it.” But by and large, English courts are not interested in fame.

In England, the court is an uncontaminated information space: There are no cameras to broadcast what happens inside, and there are strict rules to marshal what information can come in. It may be one of the few places on earth where an influencer can no longer influence; even Katy Perry, Brand’s ex-wife, had to be explained to the judge. In 2026, the closest the US has come to creating a similar environment is Taylor Swift’s wedding.

In a world of video clips, this courtroom is unclippable. What happens here is beyond the reach of rubbernecking pundits or home sleuths wanting a hot take for their socials. Unlike in modern discourse, there are rules in this court, and they are strictly enforced: Complainants in sexual cases are entitled to immediate and lifelong anonymity in the UK. Their real names and identifying details were heard in court—but mention them outside, and you risk arrest for contempt of court. Here, the defense also must ask the judge’s permission to bring up the accusers’ sexual history. When it was suspected that one blogger may have crossed the line, the judge barked at the lead prosecutor: “You’ve plenty of police officers back there…. Send one to arrest him!” They promptly did, and he was ultimately released with a caution.

Jurors, too, can never be unmasked, and their deliberations are forever secret. I sat watching them throughout the trial, but can never tell you what I observed.

From the initial charging to the conclusion of the trial, we in the British media are limited to reporting fairly and accurately only what the jury hears each day. Anyone weighing in publicly with an opinion, a prediction, or anything that could create a “substantial risk of serious prejudice or impediment” to the trial risks joining Brand in the dock of a criminal court. This meant there was no spin as Brand stepped down from the witness stand—no online reprisals against his accusers.

In court, Brand described himself as someone who had once been “staggeringly” famous. His defense argued that, in 2023, reporting from Channel 4, The Times, and The Sunday Times alleging sexual misbehavior changed that—and made everyone desert him. This, Brand said, is why only three witnesses were called to support him—two, if you exclude his wife.

“It’s not the case you’ve been completely abandoned,” wily prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones stated in cross-examination on October 28. Eight seconds of silent staring was Brand’s reply.

“You have a platform with followers in the millions, don’t you?” Silence.

“Yes,” he eventually returned, albeit quietly. Even Harold Pinter would have shouted, “Get on with it.”

Keeping up? To follow any of this is to wade through a thicket of non-sequitur arguments, florid vocabulary and, in his latest twist, the Gospels.

How has Brand’s flimflam, wrapped up in the needy personality of an entertainer who lives off clicks, landed in England’s criminal court system? Uncomfortably, I would say. Southwark is dilapidated and definitely analogue. The litigators wore robes and horsehair wigs, and the microphone on the prosecutor’s lectern was held in place with an enormous amount of yellow and black hazard duct tape. The lights went out twice because of a power cut.

If the world is now video-first, our courts are video-last. With the occasional exception of a judge’s sentencing remarks, nothing in court is photographed, filmed, or recorded for the media. Even the court artist can only take written notes, and must do their actual sketches outside.

“It’s not theater,” I heard the court clerk tell a law student who’d come to watch Brand’s trial but was annoyed to find the six public seats were full.

If this case had been undertaken in Brand’s adopted home of Florida, everyone’s evidence would have been tailored to win over cable news panel pundits. Soundbites would trump reasoned long-form arguments. The names of his accusers would likely be public—as would anything else anyone could dig up about them. Did the framers of the American Constitution really want @truecrimesleuthboy unpicking old Facebook albums of women alleging rape, or network news cameras hounding jurors on their decision?

Did you watch the Amber Heard–versus–Johnny Depp defamation trial in 2022? Were you one of the billions using #AmberTurd online as the “courtroom porn,” as Monica Lewinsky called it for Vanity Fair, was dissected, criticized, and memed? After her defeat, Heard’s lawyer spoke out in frustration: “There’s no way [the jury] couldn’t have been influenced” by the online discussion, she said. “It was horrible.”

Because of where Brand’s trial took place, his testimony could never have been turned into a similar show. In Court 3, there was no camera awaiting his reactions to what he was allegedly being subjected to. Maybe that’s why he didn’t try to pull any of that.

Brand did arrive at court with a Holy Bible bursting with index tabs. One day, when stuck in the corridor with the assembled press pack, he also uncomfortably boomed out, “This is a great day.” But for the most part, I observed him sitting tall and still and lonely in the dock. His personal bodyguard dozed in the courtroom’s family and friends section as an assistant scrolled through her phone and his father demolished a Snickers.

The only sign his group was listening to the awful things their friend/boss/son was being accused of was the very active facial expressions of Brand’s wife, Laura. “Oh, come on,” she appeared to mouth on one occasion, listening to one woman alleging rape.

There was no sign of Brand the comedian or Brand the YouTuber when the defendant took to the witness stand—though he did begin his testimony defiantly, answering the first question with a “No” so loud he seemed to shock even himself. From then on, he diminuendoed so far that the judge jumped in: “You are starting to drop your voice.”

Brand’s silences began when prosecution advocate Karmy-Jones took to her feet. A distinguished prosecutor and defender, she’s worked with and around murderers, sex offenders, and organized crooks. She’s also done time with terrible showoffs, having begun her career as a theater director. Kristin Scott Thomas or a young Lauren Bacall might play her in the film version of the trial.

Karmy-Jones was achingly polite as she unpicked what Brand called his “escalating recollection” of events. In four police interviews across 18 months, claimed Brand, he had no memory of the six women accusing him—even when given photographs, names, and some details. The British version of the Miranda warning tells suspects under caution, “You do not have to say anything. But it may harm your defense if you do not mention when questioned something which you later rely on in court.”

According to the police tapes, so-called Woman 3 did not ring a bell for him back then. But in the witness box, Brand described meeting her at a bar, recalling that a friend had said something like, “There’s a bird here who really wants to meet you.” He remembered that she had “prominent eyes,” was “lithe, elfic, pixyish,” and consented to go to the toilet for “kissing..fondling.” He was found guilty of sexually assaulting her, and acquitted on that charge of rape.

“Are you sure you aren’t piecing an account together from the evidence that was served?” Karmy-Jones asked.

Maybe the lack of spotlight and vodcaster microphone lowered his guard. This proud wordsmith did not seem ready for his words to be used against him. He wouldn’t have sexually assaulted a woman he was flirting with, Brand said. He would have been “complimentary, flirtatious, tactile.” Yet when Brand tried to drift into generalities, he was dragged back to specifics.

“Not if you met someone, Mr Brand. What was the conversation you had?” What did he mean when he said he would have been “tactile?” “Tactile means touch,” was his gently smug reply.

“Indeed it does,” Karmy-Jones returned, dragging him back to the allegation that he had grabbed the woman’s breasts.

When was the last time Brand had been spoken to like this? He did not seem to enjoy it. He even conceded there were “small details” in his evidence “that are inconsistent, and I acknowledge that.”

Perhaps you can see why Brand and his advocates didn’t attempt any “this is a deep state conspiracy sparked by my client’s vlogging about Pfizer” material on the witness stand. During the trial, he somehow managed to maneuver himself into a difficult position: insisting that despite not remembering it previously, he did have a conversation with Woman 5 about consent in which she agreed to unprotected anal sex, even though she’d just insisted their consensual vaginal sex involve a condom. “Nonsense, wasn’t it, Mr. Brand?” asked Karmy-Jones. The jury must have agreed. Brand was found guilty of this charge.

The jury was given the space to examine all this without any public discourse crowding their own thoughts out of their head. And it’s clear to the rest of us that this is preferable: A Gallup poll this year suggested just 17% of Americans have confidence in their criminal justice system. Compare that to the latest Crime Survey for England and Wales, which found 48% have confidence in how criminal justice is administered.

Our courts need physical repair, better pay, more money generally. But the fundamentals are right and working.

On one of the last days of the Brand trial, I left the court building and recognized one of the jurors standing in front of me. They had their coat on, a bag on their shoulder, and were stepping out into a cold London evening totally anonymously. A thick gaggle of paparazzi, waiting for Russell and co., were lined up at the boundary. The juror slipped through without a single flashbulb going off, without a single paparazzo glancing or realizing this person might be someone worth photographing. That is exactly how it should be.

#3724. Nintendo Shuts Down Switch 2 Jailbreak, Sending Hackers Back To Square One

On October 22, news broke that the Switch 2 had been jailbroken for the first time. This meant that it wasâkindaâpossible to mod and dump games on the machine, which in the past would have opened the floodgates to third-party operating systems being installed and an accessible piracy scene. But not this time. Due to the incredibly complicated nature of the jailbreak, the need for now-delisted sofrware SmileBASIC, and that it was software based rather than hardware, Nintendo has been able to shut it down with its latest firmware update.

In the past, Nintendo’s portable consoles have become enormously popular among homebrew developers and the piracy scene for the ease with which they could be adapted. The Nintendo DS (its most successful console until the Switch, selling 154 million units and just shy of a billion games) had the infamous R4 cart onto which ROMs could be installed, while the original model of the Nintendo Switch (157 million units, 1.6 billion games) could be jailbroken due to a hardware issue that Nintendo couldn’t patch out. These exploits didn’t appear to hinder the consoles’ successes, but Nintendo remains resolute in its fury against such actions.

By October 26, hackers had figured out how to get more out of the Switch 2’s very limited exploit, able to dump games as ROMs and dig into the console’s file systems, which would usually be the beginning of emulation plans and homebrew development. Now, however, as reported by Oatmeal Dome, all this is patched out by the device’s 23.5.0 firmware update.

The OS exploit used in the recent jailbreak has been patched in version 23.5.0.

Dumping and modding games will be impossible again from this point forward, with the exception of some cartridge games (and maybe game updates) that are released in the near future.

— OatmealDome (@OatmealDome) November 10, 2026

This is possible because the issues discovered were software based, rather than something intrinsic to the physical hardware inside the Switch 2, as had been the case for the original model of the Switch 1. There, Nintendo had to change the manufacturing, and there was little that could be done to stop Switch 1 users from taking advantage, so long as they didn’t log in to Nintendo’s online services. Of course, of the tens of millions of people who owned the Switch that could do it, vanishingly few actually did, and software sales broke all of Nintendo’s records.

Eventually the crackers will find a way, because eventually they always do, but in this case it could be many years away.

Minor spoilers ahead for Episode 2 of The Gilded Age Season 4.

Shortly after its debut, Julian Fellowes' The Gilded Age joined the ranks of HBO shows that got the world talking. Fans of Downton Abbey were thrilled at the new series set in America (streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and we're two episodes into its fourth season on the air. The show is full of Broadway royalty, and two more stars of the Great White Way have just joined the fun. So what is it going to take to get a full-blown musical episode?

The Gilded Age Season 4 started off with a bang, with fans concerned about Marian and Larry's relationship after their tryst. The Gilded Age cast is obviously full of Broadway icons, such as Audra McDonald, Kelli O'Hara, Denée Benton, Donna Murphy, and Celia Keenan-Bolger. Now we've got two more with Bonnie Milligan and Taylor Trensch joining the fun in the new season.

Milligan plays Mrs. Louisa Knapp Curtis, a journalist who is covering President Cleveland's forthcoming visit to New York. She won the Tony for her role in Kimberly Akimbo, and she also originated the role of Pamela in Head Over Heels.

Theater kids like me also likely clocked that Taylor Trensch recently made his debut on The Gilded Age as well. He's playing Oliver, the new bumbling footman for the van Rhijn household. I was first introduced to his work on stage in Bare: The Musical, but he's also been seen on Broadway in Dear Evan Hansen, Wicked, Hello, Dolly! and more. It seems like Oliver is going to be struggling with the new gig, although I'm going to be waiting for him to belt out some tunes in every scene.

With so many Broadway stars part of the massive Gilded Age cast, it feels like having a musical episode is a no-brainer. We've seen various shows have these types of specials before, including Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Scrubs, and Grey's Anatomy. None of those titles had the amount of accomplished musical theater performers that the HBO series has, so I'd imagine that The Gilded Age would blow people away if it allowed its cast to show off their vocal talents.

I'm not the only one who has been hoping to see a musical episode of The Gilded Age. While it remains to be seen if this happens, fans were treated to Voices of The Gilded Age: The Christmas Album, which features the cast of the show singing holiday tunes. That's the closest thing we've got to a musical episode for the time being, but maybe it'll help drum up excitement for that to happen in the future. Fingers crossed.

The Gilded Age airs new episodes Sundays on HBO As part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll have to see if I ever get my wish of a full-blown musical episode, but for now I'll be streaming the Christmas album.

#3722. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3720. Let’s Throw “Maxxing” Into the Dustbin of History

There was a land of Usenet forums and AOL keywords, LiveJournals and Blogspots and single-topic Tumblrs. It was called the internet, and it was a patchwork quilt sewn together by delightful little freaks—a collective fabric woven from psychologically damaged but individually discernible threads.

With time, that changed. “It had also once been the place where you sounded like yourself,” Patricia Lockwood, poet laureate of the terminally online, wrote of the internet in her wonderfully bizarre 2021 novel No One Is Talking About This. “Gradually it had become the place where we sounded like each other.”

Never has that been truer than in the wee months of 2026, when everyone suddenly woke up, unlocked their glowing rectangles, and decided to start talking like supplement-addled bridge trolls. Mogging, gooning, bonesmashing, mewing: Without rhyme, reason, or the public’s consent (funny thing about that!), incel language had fully colonized our speech. And after the takeover, no neologism was more prominent than the all-purpose suffix “-maxxing.”

We were not talking about what Cher Horowitz might do with her father’s credit card. We were using a slangier term for optimization, attaching it willy-nilly to any nouns or verbs it could plausibly describe. Working out became gymmaxxing; eating too many beans became fibermaxxing; neglecting to look at your phone for eight whole hours became sleepmaxxing. Like all good colloquialisms, the word was adaptable and edgy and undeniably fun to say. It’s got those playful and lightly pornographic double x’s, the push-pull of a hard k sound—famously the most inherently funny consonant—followed by soft sibilance and a literal “zing.”

But after a full 12 months of maxxing, I am more than ready to minn. And not least because no amount of overuse can obscure the ugly origin of 2026’s favorite syntaxx.

Back in the Gamergate era, maxxing was coined by pathetic losers on websites with names like SlutHate, where they used it to describe how they were hoping to attract women: enhancing their appearances through looksmaxxing, enhancing their social status by moneymaxxing. (Perhaps they could have started by showermaxxing.)

True, innumerable everyday expressions have uncomfortable connotations. Just ask anyone who’s absentmindedly used one of them before pausing to frantically google “Is ‘gung ho’ racist?” (answer: yes, but not in the way you might think) or “butthurt word homophobic??” (fortunately, it’s actually not). But most of those questionable expressions weren’t invented five minutes ago. It’s reasonable to expect the hoi polloi not to know the roots of words that have been grandfathered into the lexicon. Maxxing’s upsetting genesis, though, is easily traceable—and anyone who’s online enough to use it is also probably well-informed enough to know better. (Incidentally, “grandfathered in”? Also racist!)

And then, of course, there’s the death knell of all slang: repetition and co-option by both corporations and figurative bad actors. The fun was over the moment the Cheesecake Factory’s official Instagram account advised its 1.1 million followers to try “brown bread-maxxing.” It was ready for last rites by the time Trump’s Department of Homeland Security tweeted about its intention to engage in “deportationmaxing.” (Yes, with one x; given who authors these posts, you’d think they could have spelled it right.) And it was really in the ground two days after that, when The Wall Street Journal’s X account published this sentence: “The era of AI ‘tokenmaxxing’ in corporate America is over. Companies are now embracing ‘thrift-maxxing.’” At this point, we are dead horse–maxxing every time we insert the term into a new sentence, even—especially—if we’re trying to use it ironically.

Language is contagious, particularly for those who live online. In No One Is Talking About This, Lockwood bemoans internet-speak’s unparalleled ability to infect its users: “It was so tiring to have to catch each new virus, produce the perfect sneeze of it, and then mutate it into something new.” But here’s the thing: Protective measures can be taken. If your phone still autocorrects this particular word to “max inc,” there is hope. The bad news, of course, is that by the time you read this, it’s entirely possible an even worse word will have clawed out of the dark web to take its place.

I’m Fascinated By One Survivor Castaway Who Is Getting An Almost Comically Negative Edit

A Survivor 51 Castaway Is Not Pleased With Jeff Probst And Called Him Out On Social

I Think Mike Pinsky Can Still Win Survivor 51, But I’m Officially Writing Off 3 Other Castaways

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

I truly cannot believe I'd ever be this hungry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Survivor's Lewis Kelly made my stomach turn with this "wtf" story about just how hungry contestants get. I'd suspected things could get dire when I've seen players give up immunity for food, but never in a million years did I think people would consider eating food they pooped out.

As we watch him try to win it all on the 2026 TV schedule, Lewis recalled a shocking story on TikTok in which someone in the tribe made a wild suggestion after Sharonda came back with corn. He explained below:

As you know corn does not fully digest when you poop. Someone in our camp noticed that we were pooping out corn kernels and thought that we could reuse them. Wanted us to pick them out of our poo, wash them, and reboil them in a pot and see if we could get a second use out of them...That merge feast came at the perfect time I have to say.

Keep in mind, Survivor contestants are getting fed more these days than they were a long time ago. I just can't imagine who was suggesting that they genuinely pick corn out of their own fecal matter, combine it, and then boil it to serve in another meal. Literally every time I type that out, I get the urge to vomit, so I'm not sure how anyone could legitimately consider it.

Survivor's Brady Got Asked About The Peeing Thing (But I Can't Get Over How Many Times He Said Brody)

Sharonda received the corn when the Dina tribe was still together, which leads me to wonder who among them suggested such a wild thing. The only thing I can think of is that Danny Kilby has gone on the record about his love of pooping in the ocean, and how it may be his preferred way of doing that. Is there any connection between these stories? We can only speculate.

It's stories like this that make me empathize more with Survivor contestants when they crash out over not being picked to eat an Applebee's reward. I would've never thought food could be such a factor, especially when the game was reduced to 26 days, but Lewis just drove home for me how desperate things can get.

The good (and perhaps most important) part of the story is that it seemed like no one was actually game to do it. Had that post-merger feast never happened, however, we might've heard about some Brodys chowing down on some "recycled" corn in a later meal. And here I thought grubs were the grossest thing someone could eat when playing Survivor.

As disgusting as it was, I do love hearing cast members tell these stories from Survivor 51 that we didn't see in the episodes. With only 90 minutes (including commercials) to tell the story each week, it's totally understandable that something like this would fall by the wayside. Had the tribe actually gone through it and done it, however, I would be upset if it was left on the cutting room floor.

Survivor continues on CBS on Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. With the remaining cast formed under one tribe, I can't wait to see what new alliances are forged. I'm also so invested in trying to figure out who won this season, because I'm still not entirely sure who is getting the winner's edit.

#3717. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3716. Report: James Gunn Ousted Amid Messy Power Struggle Despite Superman’s Success

ClayfaceDC StudiosJames GunnPeter SafranSupergirlSuperman

Yesterday, James Gunn and Peter Safran stepped down from their positions as co-presidents at DC Studios. This was after just four years on the job and only three movies in the new superhero cinematic universe they were overseeing. The pair has now been replaced by ex-Marvel producer Jeremy Latcham, whose evangelical history has given some DC fans pause. So what happened? According to a new report by The Hollywood Reporter, trouble had been brewing for the pair as soon as the Skydance merger went through earlier this year.

According to THR‘s sources, on Friday, November 6, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz informed the pair that, despite previously being told they would be part of the company moving forward, there had been a “change of plans.” The shake-up had reportedly been in the works since “early fall,” with Latcham having been contacted about potentially taking over DC Studios by Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chair John Greenstein, who worked with Latcham during his time at Marvel.

THR says that there were multiple points of “tension” between Gunn and Safran on one hand and the Skydance execs on the other. Gunn and Safran initially reported directly to Warner Bros. CEO David Zaslav, and their contracts said they would maintain that kind of direct reporting structure even in the event of a change in leadership, so they would have reported to Ellison following the merger. Meanwhile, Greenstein and co-chair Dana Goldberg were reportedly trying to consolidate movie production under their leadership, while Gunn and Safran had grown “accustomed to having strong control” over anything under the DC Studios banner.

Other points of contention included that Gunn and Safran were reportedly âslowâ and “not forthcoming” in sharing plans and footage with the Skydance leads.

Many will point to Supergirl‘s box office bomb as a sticking point, and I’ve even seen a lot of people joke that Gunn and Safran only got “one bad movie” before they were thrown out. While Supergirl‘s performance is noted as a problem by THR‘s sources, apparently even their biggest hit, Superman, wasn’t doing enough in the eyes of their corporate overlords. That film, which grossed $618 million on a $225 budget, “did not net out, or have the kind of pop culture impact, in the way that kind of movie should,” in the eyes of Skydance.

Sources say that Gunn is “somewhat relieved” to be out of the business side of things and now focusing on filmmaking. His DC next film, Man of Tomorrow, is set to premiere next year.

As for Latcham, THR‘s sources call him a “down-the-middle shooter” who is more concerned with making “hits for the masses” than Gunn, whose projects often feature somewhat profane writing and obscure characters.

Clayface, the last DC Studios project produced while Gunn and Safran were company co-presidents, is in theaters now.

#3715. Porsha Williams Brings 'Unbothered' Energy to 'Real Housewives of Atlanta'

Porsha Williams has had quite the fill of juicy drama in Atlanta, but after a cross-country trip with some of Bravo’s most legendary Housewives, this Georgia peach is coming home with thicker skin and a much harder-to-bruise attitude.

The Real Housewives of Atlanta star, 45, exclusively told Us how filming The Real Housewives Ultimate Girls Trip: Roaring 20th taught her that a little shade doesn’t have to leave a bitter taste, especially when surrounded by women who know how to hold their own.

“What I took from doing the show with them is the confidence that each lady had because these are the best of the best from each city,” Williams told Us, referring to costars Gizelle Bryant, Teresa Giudice, Luann de Lesseps and Kyle Richards. “ I took their confidence and I took them being unbothered with me back to Atlanta.”

Although Williams is notorious for squashing digs with her signature line, “Who said that?”, fans watched her decades-long friendship with Shamea Morton sour during season 16 of RHOA after Morton, 44, became a full-time member of the franchise.

Ahead of season 17, Williams said she had hoped for a fresh start, previously sharing with Us in April that she wanted to put prior conflicts aside and welcome new friendships. “I just wanted a clean slate, and I wanted to have a good time. I wanted to be open to new friendships… and have this season feel like a breath of fresh air,” she said at the time.

That hope was tested when tensions continued to boil over into season 17 during a cast trip to Scotland, where the two officially declared their friendship was over after a heated dinner exchange—a rift that remained unresolved at the reunion.

Rather than promising a drama-free future, Williams said she’s trying to draw a line between playful disses and personal attacks, with a new focus on fostering sisterhood rather than fueling conflict.

“I’m also taking from Ultimate Girls Trip a lighter tone for the season,” Williams told Us.” I’m trying to set that in everything that I do. It’s not always about going below the belt and, like, ruining somebody’s life or career. So I’m bringing back fun shade.”

With hopes of taking a fuzzier approach to navigating on-screen battles in season 18, Williams says her standards were set long before she ever held a peach, and she’s equally intentional about what she hopes to pass down to her 7-year-old daughter, Pilar Jhena McKinley.

“[The] No. 1 thing for me as a mom and being a mom to a beautiful child like Pilar is to make sure that she feels good about what she does,” Williams said. “I let her speak life into herself, which helps her build her own confidence in anything that she does. So it’s not just someone telling her that she’s great, or someone telling her she’s had high standards, she knows it for herself.”

During Charmin’s Wider Sheet Immersive NYC Experience, where the reality TV star partnered with Charmin Ultra Strong to celebrate the brand’s newest innovation, she recalled how her mother, Diane Williams (Ms. Diane), instilled high expectations in her from an early age — right down to toilet paper.

“I think I was born with high standards, and then I just started raising them above and above and above,” she told Us. “I don’t think I’ve ever really had low standards.”

The mother of one also credits her younger sister, Lauren Williams, with how she raises her own daughter, revealing that watching how they encouraged their own children helped develop her understanding of self-worth.

“In my world of reality TV, often people feel like, ‘oh, it’s what you tell me I am’, no, it’s not. It’s what I say I am,” Williams told Us. “It’s how I say I feel about me, and so my life lessons, my little sister, my mom, they helped me parent very well for Pilar.”

#3714. Bonfire of the Neocons: The MAGA Finger-Pointing Begins

Good afternoon from Washington, where foie gras is now illegal and the local Stasi is going door-to-door to check that every citizen has downloaded Bluesky.

The town, one of the bluest in the country, is in a state of stunned ecstasy as it struggles to process the mind-bending midterm election results. Democrats won the House, the Senate, and a majority of governorships, penetrating deep into historically red strongholds like Texas, Kansas, Mississippi, and South Carolina. During a book party for Sophia Bush at The Jefferson hotel on Wednesday night, the actor nearly cried as she delivered a toast to the results—and to her new bestseller.

On the right, the finger-pointing has already begun. In this edition of Party Animals, you can read my dispatch from a night out with the DC Republicans in mourning and the Democrats celebrating in cocktail-fueled delirium. Plus, a MAGA civil war reignites over Iran, with Vice President JD Vance already wading into the factional fight that could determine the future of the party.

Also mentioned in this issue: Marc Thiessen, Curt Mills, Darline Graham, Ken Paxton, Greg Abbott, James Talarico, Annie Andrews, Mark Mitchell, Matt Walsh, and more.

Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be drowned in cocktail-fueled delirium. Praise will be run as a Democrat south of the Mason-Dixon Line.

The morning after the generational Republican midterm collapse that Party Animals is dubbing Blue Tuesday, JD Vance put on his political-analyst cap. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in a lengthy X post. “The president himself said so last night.”

Never mind that Vance’s referenced war is one that his own administration started and is currently presiding over. Vance has often tried to cast himself as an outside observer of the Trump administration, its preeminent reply guy on social media and podcasts—a clever, if often ludicrous, pose for the vice president.

The Vance post was the highest-level opening salvo in a civil war that had been brewing for some time. It erupted into the open on Tuesday night as the results began to spell doom for Republicans and the blame started flying with velocity. The internecine battle is between the “America First” faction of the Trump movement and those who have supported the war in Iran, the latter labeled by detractors—with a sneer—as neocons.

The day before the blue tsunami, hopeful MAGA devotees attended a campaign rally in Ohio.

“The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” wrote Matt Walsh in a post on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.” As the dire results came down, even some on the right who had cheered on the war came to see, in the cold glow of their screens, the political devastation it had wrought. “Iran War is clearly catastrophically unpopular and has to end,” posted Will Chamberlain, who had spent the last few months loudly dismissing the war’s critics as subliterate simpletons.

On social media, MAGA luminaries shared a screenshot of an infamous op-ed written by Iran war booster Marc Thiessen, whose headline confidently claimed earlier this year: “There is no US downside to striking the Iranian regime.” Fox host Mark Levin lashed out at critics blasting his support for the war, insisting it had nothing to do with the results. Reality would seem to differ. One NBC News exit poll found that 74% of voters said Iran was a “crucial or major factor in how they voted.”

“It was the Iran war, stupid,” said Curt Mills, the executive director of The American Conservative, in an interview with Party Animals. Speaking about Thiessen and Levin, Mills was unsparing: “Professional liars. Professional liars. Not analysts, not honest people, and, honestly, not very invested in the future of the country.”

I asked Mills, who praised Vance’s statement, if it was not strange for the vice president to speak out against the administration while serving in it. “What option does he really have if he wants to keep his job, stop the war, and maybe run for president? I mean, it is strange. It is unprecedented in some ways,” he said. “Is it working? Maybe.”

In restaurants and barrooms across the capital, the ruling party’s apparatchiks watched and agonized as Democrats mounted a historic midterms rout.

The How: The Wall Street Journal’s Josh Dawsey and colleagues have the definitive account of how Trump lost the midterms for Republicans, packed with genuinely shocking reporting that reveals exactly what went wrong at each turn.

Rockstud the Vote: My colleague José Criales-Unzueta trained his gimlet eye on a photo posted by Free Press reporter Olivia Reingold from a Democratic election night party in Michigan and found some suspicious discrepancies in the leather straps of a smoking heel.

Ballroom Blues: Read Shawn McCreesh’s New York Times dispatch from Trump’s strange walk of shame around the White House ballroom construction site the morning after the midterms. “Inside his concrete chrysalis,” McCreesh writes, “everything was still beautiful.” 💔

Department of (Deeply Unpopular) War: Amid a flurry of anonymous quotes from Trump officials and allies laying blame for the midterms on Pete Hegseth, the president tells Jonathan Karl of ABC News that he’s standing by his defense secretary—for now, at least.

Of Mics and Men: In the wake of Patrick Bet-David’s election night stream, Vanity Fair’s Dan Adler has a biting eulogy for the manosphere: “Donald Trump’s 2024 tour of the Joe Rogan–dominated podcast circuit heralded the makings of a new mainstream media. But in the MAGA midterm wreckage, the idea of the manosphere as a political force has shattered.”

A Few Good Streamers: VF’s Abigail Sylvor Greenberg spoke with Hasan Piker and his lawyer, who promised that Piker’s $75 million defamation lawsuit against Scott Jennings is only the beginning.

Russell Brand trial: The star comedian turned right-wing podcast lounge lizard was found guilty in a London court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Musk in the barrel: Elon Musk, who just torched nearly half a billion dollars in an effort to keep Republicans in power, now faces the wrath of Democrats. The New York Times has a handy guide to the coming storm. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” said Senator Ed Markey.
