#3590. Exclusive: ‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte, in His Own Words

For those of us who managed to land a role on Breaking Bad, the show is a formative part of our lives. It represented a chance to work on what is now considered one of the best shows TV has ever seen, and the cast and crew forged an unbreakable bond. RJ Mitte was part of the show’s heartbeat. When I spoke to him for this book, we reflected on our days shooting in New Mexico fondly.

I’ll always remember him as a young kid—bright, talented, and a real sweetheart—who was so thrilled to be on set with us that it reminded us how lucky we all were. We'll all miss him dearly. Rest in peace, RJ. —Dean Norris

The last person to join the White family was RJ Mitte, cast in the role of Walt Jr., aka “Flynn.” RJ, who was only fourteen years old at the time, joined the project after we had already begun filming the pilot, following multiple rounds of auditions stretching out over several months. You might wonder why casting Walt Jr., a comparatively minor character among the core cast, took so long. Well, it was about verisimilitude. As written, Walt Jr. had cerebral palsy, albeit a relatively minor case. It was a fundamental part of the character, and Vince was adamant that the role not be played by a nondisabled actor.

VINCE GILLIGAN, creator: I was worried at the beginning that people wouldn’t connect with Walt. They’d say, Why is this guy doing this terrible thing? And so I kind of loaded him up for bear in terms of, you know, he had a son with cerebral palsy. You felt bad for him. People bullied him.

SHARON BIALY, casting director: We had a lot of autonomy with casting, once we knew what Vince was looking for, once we all agreed that, aesthetically, we were talking about the same type of actor. A case in point is RJ Mitte’s role. Vince only wanted actors who had CP. So, we conducted a nationwide search.

RJ MITTE, Walt Jr.: Walt Jr. is actually based on a real person, a friend of Vince’s from college who had cerebral palsy. So, Vince was really particular about the role of Walt Jr. and who was going to play him.

Experienced actors who also have mild CP is not the deepest pool, of course, but there are more candidates than you might expect. And RJ Mitte’s casting has to be considered something of a surprise, given his relative lack of experience and a variety of other challenges he faced while growing up.

RJ MITTE: We were living in Houston when my sister got discovered at a water park, and that’s what brought us to LA. My sister got booked on a job at Universal Studios for an ad campaign. She was one and a half at the time. We really didn’t have a lot going on. Things were tough. My mom was a single mom, and she had recently been partially paralyzed in a car accident, and my grandparents, who I was very close to, were both sick and dying, so when we got this offer to go to LA, we took it. It was a paid trip. They put us up in a motel in Hollywood—there was a strip club on one side, and a Ralphs and a library on the other side. That’s LA.

Everything was covered for six months, so I just started acting to meet kids my own age and have a little extra cash while we were there. And it ended up turning into a career for me. I started working at a young age, not in the acting industry, but with my uncle and family jobs and stuff to make money as a young kid. I would like to think I grew up with a strong work ethic. So, when we got to LA, I hit the ground running. Within the first six months, I was on shows like Hannah Montana, Everybody Hates Chris, Weeds, Seventh Heaven, Drillbit Taylor, Epic Movie—­ all as an extra. I think that really helped prepare me for Breaking Bad, just with the quality of work and the type of professionalism that the set had. I’m very grateful, because if I did not get Breaking Bad, I wouldn’t have an acting career.

At any number of points along the journey, RJ’s dream could have died. It’s hard enough for a known actor to land a role in a show of this quality, but for a newcomer, it must have been daunting, although you never would have known it by the way he carried himself on set.

RJ MITTE: Funny story: My very first audition ever in my career was an anti­ meth campaign for the state of California. It was a wild PSA, and I ended up not getting it. A year or so later, I started auditioning for Breaking Bad. The description of the role literally said, “dark hair, big eyebrows, and mild cerebral palsy.” And I was like, that’s me!

Sharon Bialy called me in, and I already had been on quite a few auditions by that point, and I didn’t book any of them, so I knew what rejection felt like. I had a sense of, Don’t hold your breath. But I’m a firm believer that you go in owning it and when you walk out, don’t look back. Every callback was a little more like, Wait, I’m actually still in the running.

Walt Jr. had a somewhat more severe case of CP than RJ, who did not use assistive devices for mobility in real life.

RJ MITTE: When I went in for my first audition, Sharon was there, and she had hurt her foot. So, she actually handed me her crutches that she was using for the audition. Six months went by, four callbacks, four auditions, and in that final one, they’re like, Okay, we’re sending you. You’re going to New Mexico. The next day I was on a 6 a.m. flight to audition for Vince and the team. Then he excused me for a moment and brought me back in to do my test screening with Anna and Bryan.

Think about that. RJ was fourteen years old and trying to land a job that would change his life, a job that would help him support his entire family. Talk about pressure.

RJ MITTE: I think in life I’ve always had pressure. It really didn’t stand out to me too much. I can only do what I can do. And so as long as I’m doing my best, that’s what matters. But it always kind of felt like I was part of the team to some degree, even when I wasn’t. And so when it came to doing the scene with Anna and Bryan, it really felt like a family. It was like, Oh, yeah, this feels right. Apparently, they must have had the same feeling because they hired me.

Like everyone else, RJ made the most of his opportunity and crafted a fully formed portrait of an adolescent at the center of a family storm; one whose disability may have helped shape him but did not define who he was.

RJ MITTE: This was the first time I think people really saw a character with a disability who wasn’t disabled. There’s nothing he couldn’t do that other kids were doing. It wasn’t about the disability, and that’s something that I think Vince really stressed: it’s not about his disability; it’s about being a part of the family and living with it.

Six seasons in, Breaking Bad reached its apotheosis with the monumental episode “Ozymandias,” in which Walter White’s house of cards comes crashing down. It’s also the episode where Flynn learns the truth about his father’s double life, and that Walt has led my character—his brother-in-law, Hank—to his death. The episode builds to a climactic moment where Flynn’s mother, Skyler, grabs a knife and brandishes it at her husband.

RIAN JOHNSON, director, “Ozymandias”: The actual fight itself, I remember being surprisingly fun to shoot—­just making sure to give Anna and Bryan the space that they needed to find it. I think RJ also did a terrific job in that moment—­ he’s kind of the linchpin of the whole thing.

It is indeed Flynn who rises to the occasion. When Walt wrestles the knife away from Skyler, his son jumps on top of him and throws him across the room. He’s a big kid, strong enough to handle Walt despite his disability; strong enough to protect his mother.

RJ MITTE: It was very intense to shoot. At the same time, we’re professionals. Everything was very choreographed. There was one moment when we first started, I got so heated, and so into it, that I kind of accidentally grabbed Bryan the wrong way and kind of like tossed him . . . wrong. And everyone was like, “Whoa, RJ! You can’t throw him like that.” And I was like, “Oh, I’m so sorry. I just got caught up in the moment.”

RIAN JOHNSON: When you see Walt Jr. turn, then you know it’s truly over. And Bryan’s reaction to that just breaks my heart every time I see it.

In the series’s penultimate episode, Walt clandestinely calls Flynn at school. A package is on its way, he says, to be delivered to the home of one of Flynn’s friends. The package contains money, one hundred thousand dollars—­the most he could stuff into one box. “I wanted to give you so much more, but this is all I could do,” Walt explains, leaning into the pay phone as Flynn listens, wordlessly, on the other end.

RJ MITTE: I remember at the time we were shooting that scene it was in this school-slash-doctor’s-office that we were using. Bryan was in the room with me when we did this part. It definitely was heartbreaking to have to feel that way about someone that I admire. And I think that’s what Junior felt as well. I’m a believer that in life, there’s always a moment where you have to choose to either be an adult or to stay a child. This moment comes in many different forms, but it comes down to that moment where you say, Am I going to accept this and give them what they want and be submissive, and still have that child aspect of who I am? Or am I going to take charge and become the person that I need to be—­ the man, the adult?

RJ does some terrific wordless acting in this scene, wrestling with this decision. Then he speaks: “Just shut up! Just stop it. Stop it. I don’t want anything from you.”

“You need this money,” Walt says. “Your mother needs this money. It can’t all be for nothing.”

Yes, it can, as Flynn makes abundantly clear.

RJ MITTE: A lot of the decisions I made for Junior were based on my own experiences as a young adult. At the time I was still a child, but I utilized those moments from my own life of having to stand my ground and make that decision—­ realizing who I am and what I need to do to take care and provide for my family. In the show, Walt was no longer doing that. He was actually creating more danger for his family.

I think it’s very powerful that Walt Jr. had the ability to stand his ground, and to put those boundaries in place: “You’re out. This is my family now, and you’re not a part of it.” I find a lot of young men and women have to take that stance at some point, especially with parents or family figures that live in a volatile world, a world that is corrupt.

Later, in the series finale, Walt is standing over a crib, caressing the hair of baby Holly as she naps. He leaves and then watches from a distance as Flynn gets off a school bus and walks into the apartment.

VINCE GILLIGAN: With Walt, you want him to have a goodbye scene with his wife. We were sad we couldn’t have a goodbye scene with his son, Walt Jr., because RJ is a wonderful actor. We just didn’t have the room.

For those of us who were fortunate enough to be a part of it, Breaking Bad remains a seminal event in our lives, both personally and professionally—­ an opportunity to work on one of the greatest television shows in history, alongside people who became lifelong friends.

BRYAN CRANSTON: I knew when it ended that this was the role of my life.

AARON PAUL: I think I can speak for everyone involved in the show: It changed all of our lives.

RJ MITTE: I will be eighty years old in a nursing home and there will probably be someone looking at me through a window, saying, “There’s Walt Jr.” And I’m okay with that.

#3589. David Carradine Faced Off Against An Action Legend In A Forgotten 1983 Neo-Western

David Carradine came to prominence playing a martial arts master so it was only right that he eventually found himself in a duel with the great Chuck Norris. As Shaolin monk Kwai Chang Caine in "Kung Fu," Carradine traveled the Old West facing down all manner of challenger. But he never reckoned with the might of a solitary Texas Ranger with a deadly aim — that is, until 1983's "Lone Wolf McQuade," which saw Carradine and Norris do battle in what was one of the better projects of the 1980s for both actors.

By 1983, Carradine had come a long way from his TV debut in the short-lived Western series "Shane." Having become a household name thanks to "Kung Fu," the actor tried to subvert audience expectations by appearing in a number of exploitation flicks and B-movies. More well-known 1970s examples include "Cannonball," "Death Race 2000," and "Deathsport." In the 1980s, however, Carradine was basically churning out direct-to-video fare, and in "Lone Wolf McQuade" he came face to face with the king of schlocky DTV actioners, Chuck Norris.

The neo-western was directed by Steve Carver, who'd worked at Roger Corman's New World Pictures at the same time Carradine had fronted several of the studio's features in the 1970s. With "Lone Wolf McQuade," Carver paid homage to the Spaghetti Westerns that had helped move the Western genre into its revisionist era. As such, there was a self-aware aspect to the movie, which knew exactly what it was and wasn't about to apologize for it. The final showdown between its two stars was emblematic of its excess and was, it turns out, a lot more real than you might imagine. In fact, Carradine and Norris seemingly gave everything they had to their climactic battle and ended up injuring themselves.

"Lone Wolf McQuade" isn't the type of '80s actioner that gets mentioned alongside such legendary features as "First Blood" or "Die Hard." But it's also not the kind of movie that should be lumped in with the worst examples of the decades' bombastic nonsense. In fact, it's easily one of the best Chuck Norris movies, and in its unapologetic embrace of the uber macho ethos of the era and its reverence for the great Spaghetti Westerns, manages to turn it into a sort of paean to both the golden age of action cinema the influential films that preceded it.

That's not to say the film is some sort of artistic masterwork. This is, at the end of the day, a film in which Norris and David Carradine beat each other senseless for our entertainment. "Lone Wolf McQuade" stars the former as Texas Ranger Jim "J.J." McQuade, an ex-Marine who is the epitome of the '80s action stereotype: a lone wolf lawman who routinely flouts the rules and lives a solitary existence in the wake of his divorce. Oh, and he also literally has a pet wolf.

The film follows McQuade as he tangles with David Carradine's Rawley Wilkes, an arms dealer who also happens to be a martial arts expert. It seems Carradine's Kung Fu specialist is selling weapons to terrorists, and J.J. isn't about to let that go unpunished. When Wilkes captures his daughter, Sally McQuade (Dana Kimmell), he all but guarantees a confrontation with J.J., which is exactly what we get in the film's climactic moments. That particular battle is a protracted slog in which Norris and Carradine go all out.

In a 1990 issue of Psychotronic Video (via archive.org), David Carradine recalled his showdown with Chuck Norris in "Lone Wolf McQuade." Neither actor opted to use a stunt double, making for what sounds like a brutal on-set experience. "We worked on that fight for four days," he said. "We shot it for four days. And we were little old men by the end of it. All our old injuries came back, we got new injuries, and we were stumbling around like little old men."

According to the actor, he and his co-star needed canes and crutches by the end of shooting their fight, which in Carradine's recollection was the result of Norris wanting to outdo his famous showdown with Bruce Lee in 1972's "The Way of the Dragon." "We were actually trying to go beyond that," continued Carradine. "I think we did. I think photographically we didn't. But as far as the fight was concerned, the combination of the two styles, you know, because I was very flowing and loose, and he was very solid and hard, I think we accomplished what we set out to do."

I'm fairly confident in saying that Jim "J.J." McQuade vs. Rawley Wilkes was not, in fact, quite as memorable as Tang Lung vs. Colt. But it was an impressive ending to one of Norris' best films and reminder of the physical talent that had made Carradine a star a decade prior.

#3588. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

It's one of the most authentically queer movies I've ever seen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

2026 has been a solid year for movies, with smaller-budget movies like Obsession managing to make it big at the box office. There were also a number of daring new A24 movies, and that studio is offering another daring entry with Jordan Firstman's Club Kid. I was able to catch an early screening of the dramedy, which had me laughing and crying in equal measures throughout its brisk 121-minute runtime. Club Kid is my favorite movie of the entire year (so far), and I'm truly obsessed with its portrayal of gay nightlife.

Over the past few years, there's been a ton of conversation about the importance of LGBTQ+ representation in the media. While we got a steamy book-to-screen adaptation with Heated Rivalry, Club Kid offers an incredibly authentic look at nightlife in the community, warts and all. As a gay man in my mid-30s, I thought it was impressive how the depictions were, allowing me to relate intimately with this acclaimed new film.

Jordan Firstman is the writer, director and star of Club Kid, and deserves all the flowers he's received at festivals like Cannes and TIFF. While audiences might know him from his scene-stealing roles in English Teacher (streaming with a Hulu subscription) and Ms. Marvel, he takes center stage as protagonist Peter. He's a party promoter and habitual drug user who has been raging in the New York City nightlife scene for a decade, and is feeling the effects that his nocturnal proclivities take on him.

When Peter is fired from his job and arguably at his lowest, he's surprised to learn he has a son named Arlo (Reggie Absolom), the result of having sex with a woman in a darkroom years ago. What follows is a grittier take on Big Daddy, and we watch Peter and his son bond when he's suddenly dropped off at his door following the death of Arlo's mother.

Throughout the movie, we're shown an unapologetic and unfiltered look at the gay nightlife scene, including the drug use that can often accompany it. The movie's opening sequence shows Peter at the height of his career as a promoter. I was immediately struck by how real the club scene was, showing the various mini-conversations that happen in a crowded bar. Peter and his friends also engage in a mixture of drugs, especially GHB, ketamine and cocaine. It's when he's crossfaded that he eventually has sex with a woman, in a scene set in the venue's darkroom, where folks go to engage in anonymous sex.

Darkrooms have a long history in the LGBTQ+ community, and have been portrayed onscreen in projects like Harvey Fierstein's Torch Song Trilogy. While some audiences might balk at the scene in Club Kid, I have to applaud Firstman for showing them in such a real way, potentially educating straight moviegoers in the process.

Peter's relationship with drugs is also a major part of this movie, and I once again was shocked by how close to home it felt. I've seen firsthand how alluring and insidious drug use can be in nightlife, and have lost friends to it. Firstman's protagonist is given reason to change his lifestyle when he suddenly becomes a parent, but there are so many queer folks who are never able to separate themselves from the scene. While I've never had the experience of meeting a child I didn't know I had, I couldn't help but relate to the story told throughout the film.

Club Kid gets its wide theatrical release November 6th as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll have to see if another movie manages to beat it as my favorite movie of the year... but I doubt it. Now let Jordan Firstman direct whatever else he wants.

#3586. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3585. 5 Possible Reasons Behind James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Exit

The hierarchy of power in the DC Universe is about to change. The Paramount/Warner Bros. Discovery merger was recently made official, with a new mega-corporation, Skydance, emerging on the other side. As a result, major changes are being made at all of the companies under the corporation's umbrella, and those changes have come for DC Studios.

In a surprise move, James Gunn and Peter Safran are exiting as co-heads of DC Studios, with former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham taking over. What this means for the future of the DC Universe that Gunn and Safran have been building together since 2022 remains to be seen, but this is one of the bigger shake-ups in the realm of superheroes and comic book happenings in a long time.

For now, we have more questions than answers, and the biggest question on everyone's minds right now is what, exactly, prompted the divorce between Gunn, Safran, and DC Studios. While we don't have a definitive answer yet, there are some strong possible reasons for the man behind Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" trilogy and his trusted producing pal to exit the company.

We're going to look at some of those reasons as we try to make sense of what just happened and what might come next. Let's get into it.

In early 2023, when James Gunn announced the first chapter of the new DC Universe and called it "Gods and Monsters," it was clear the idea was for DC Studios to focus on characters other than Batman, Superman, and Wonder Woman. Yes, Gunn was going to direct "Superman," but projects like "Swamp Thing" and "The Authority" were also in the mix. Many of the projects have yet to come to fruition, but others, such as "Clayface," have. They've delivered mixed results.

Gunn and Safran weren't focusing all that much on A-list DC characters at the time. A new Batman is due to debut in "The Brave and the Bold," but that movie doesn't even have a release date, and Gunn has confirmed that Robert Pattinson's Batman won't join the new DCU. It admittedly complicates matters with "The Batman Part II" now in production. All the same, the new DCU absolutely needs a Batman. It needs a Wonder Woman. It needs A-listers.

Skydance is now a mega-corporation that is tens of billions of dollars in debt. On paper, it might be good to have a movie like "Clayface" make well over $100 million on a $44 million budget. But that's relatively small potatoes compared to what a "Batman" movie can make. Skydance wants to focus more on those A-list characters. Right or wrong, the company is likely eager to get a new Wonder Woman on screen and a new Batman cast to exist alongside David Corenswet's Superman.

There may well be room for movies like "Swamp Thing" or "The Authority," but not before the A-listers get sorted out. Again, this is speculative, but since IP is still king in Hollywood, there's good reason to believe the brass is looking at DC with more urgency in this regard.

We can have creative discussions all day, and undoubtedly, people will be sharing a lot of opinions on what James Gunn and Peter Safran have produced during their time as the heads of DC Studios. However, at the end of the day, Hollywood is a business, and from a business perspective, the box office returns just haven't been good enough. In particular, "Supergirl" is a glaring issue that needed to be addressed.

Gunn's "Superman" was the biggest comic book movie of 2025 at the box office with $618 million, but that was still less than Zack Snyder's "Man of Steel" ($670 million) did 13 years earlier, unadjusted for inflation. It was a promising enough start, but not a resoundingly great one. Superhero movies are no longer automatically successful in theaters like they were in the 2010s, which certainly doesn't make things any easier. All the same, results are not just expected, but needed to justify the sky-high budgets for these blockbusters.

"Supergirl" flopped at the box office earlier this year, taking in just $126 million worldwide on a $170 million budget against mixed reviews. While Supergirl isn't quite an A-list character, she's a heck of a lot bigger than Clayface or Peacemaker. The fact that the movie bombed in such high-profile fashion was not a good look for DC Studios. Ultimately, it reflects back on Gunn and Safran, even though Craig Gillespie was in the director's chair.

In truth, DC is in the midst of one of the biggest box office bad streaks ever. The misses far outweigh the hits. Not all of that can be placed on Gunn and Safran, but something needs to change. Relatively modest hits like "Clayface" aren't going to cut it forever.

James Gunn worked as a smaller filmmaker for years before he ascended to Hollywood's A-list. When "Guardians of the Galaxy" became Marvel's most unlikely box office smash hit, everything changed. That eventually led to him becoming a studio head, but occupying an executive suite was never his ambition. He wanted to be a director. Put simply, it sounds very much like Gunn didn't want to be a Hollywood executive anymore.

After the news about his exit broke, Gunn explained his departure as DC Studios' co-head and his statement made it seem like the job was very taxing on his personal life, as well as his creative life. "DC Studios has been trying, to say the least," he said. "I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job."

Gunn also noted that he had a tough time "dividing my time between projects I'm incredibly passionate about and the ones I'm not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

Not to say that there weren't other factors involved, but if we take Gunn at his word, the last four years have been pretty difficult for him. He wasn't just making giant movies like "Superman" and next year's "Man of Tomorrow," but he's been creatively managing all of the output at DC Studios. It's not terribly hard to see why he might want to go back to just being a writer and director.

There's no telling what has been going on behind closed doors at Skydance ever since the merger went through. CEO David Ellison has his own ideas of how he wants the company, and its various divisions, to run. Ellison isn't the guy who launched DC Studios when James Gunn and Peter Safran's new division started at Warner Bros. It's entirely possible there was a bit of a culture clash.

It's certainly interesting to note that Both Gunn and Safran were announced as part of the executive structure at Skydance after the Warner Bros./Paramount merger was made official. That was just a few weeks ago. Would Ellison have announced them as part of the new company if the plan was to move on and have Jeremy Latcham take over? It's hard to imagine. That implies that something may have happened in recent weeks that prompted the exit.

What could that be? There are a lot of moving parts. Ellison, as well as his new film chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, undoubtedly had their own ideas about how to handle things at DC Studios. If Gunn and/or Safran bumped up against them in ways they didn't with the previous regime, it's not hard to imagine the camel's back breaking under the weight of one too many straws.

Without aimlessly speculating as to what they all could have disagreed about, it seems probable that if all sides got along and shared a vision for the future, they could have figured something out.

DC Studios was under the Warner Bros. umbrella, but it seemed like James Gunn and Peter Safran were granted a great deal of creative freedom to shape this new DC Universe as they saw fit. There's virtually no question that Skydance, David Ellison, and the rest of the new brass at the studio have their own ideas about what to do with the treasure trove of IP that is the DC Comics library. It's not hard to surmise that Skydance's ideas didn't align with Gunn and Safran's intended plans.

James Gunn's DC Universe plans shifted after Warner Bros.' initial announcement, but that never meant that Gunn and Safran lost control of the ship. They were steering. They were making sure things were lining up for eventual, future plans. Those plans haven't fully revealed themselves (and we may never know the full scope of what they wanted to do), but it's clear there was an ultimate plan in place.

If Skydance has different ideas (and it feels safe to assume they do), that would complicate matters. If Gunn and Safran spent years building out this slate only to have to bend to what the new leadership wants, that would be frustrating. Without putting words in anyone's mouth, it could even be taken as an insult.

Again, I'm not here to recklessly speculate, but these two guys had a vision that Warner Bros. bought into. If Skydance doesn't share that vision, or something close to it, Gunn and Safran making their way to the exit door makes a lot of sense.

#3584. Warhammer Survivors Isn’t Good Enough to Be a Vampire Survivors Replacement

Good clones are the sincerest form of flattery

Vampire Survivors and its plethora of clones are always more fun in hour ten than hour one. The passive nature of the auto-attack gameplay means this style of experience lives or dies by how fun and visually over-the-top the action can get once you upgrade your character, gain access to more weapons, and manage to survive long enough to level up or evolve your weapons.

I did eventually hit that point of satisfaction with Warhammer Survivors, which was developed by Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 studio Auroch Digital with help from Vampire Survivors creator Poncle. When I got to the point where I could rip and tear through enemies with a Typhoon Crossbow as followers with upgraded weapons of their own fired at enemies around it, the game offered spectacle worthy of the Warhammer and Survivors names. But getting there doesn’t feel quite as good as its inspiration.

Warhammer Survivors doesn’t contain any sort of important lore to speak of; it’s more of a hodgepodge of various recognizable Warhammer characters (like Boltgun’s Malum Caedo) fighting against waves of unrelenting creatures from both eras of the franchise. Warhammer Survivors is essentially two games in one, with one half based on the sci-fi Warhammer 40,000 and the other on the more fantasy-like Warhammer: Age of Sigmar.

Each half of Warhammer Survivors has unique characters, weapons, enhancements, and objectives to unlock, but the core gameplay loop of each is the same. As a player, all you have to do is walk around levels as your character automatically attacks. Enemies drop experience when they die most of the time, and you collect that to level up and upgrade all of the weapons that you have equipped. Considering Poncle was directly involved with this game, it’s not surprising that Warhammer Survivors does not do much to hide its inspiration or reinvent the formula.

The most unique gimmick here is a follower feature, which solves for the fact that Warhammer Survivors’ characters are connected to factions that only let them use specific weapons. Rather than one character wielding every weapon and upgrading at once, sometimes you can save or summon another character that uses a different weapon to fight alongside you. This feels fitting for the large-scale battles Warhammer is known for. Yet in practice, all it really does is add an additional layer to a choice you were already going to make regardless.

It shouldn’t be too surprising that what you’re getting with this game is Vampire Survivors with a Warhammer coat of paint, even if it does go a bit deeper than Vampire Survivors’ typical crossover DLC. Vampire Survivors is a great game, and Warhammer Survivors is a good one too. That said, I won’t herald Warhammer Survivors as some amazing replacement for that indie classic, because there are some things it doesn’t do quite as well as the original.

Survivors games are all about snowballing power, building up to a chaotic storm of attacks. In Vampire Survivors, almost every weapon has auto aim and will hit something in range when used. But that’s not the case for certain early-game weapons in Warhammer Survivors that shoot the direction the player is facing, like the Boltgun. Those simply don’t mesh well with the auto-attacking gameplay.

The lack of auto-aim on these weapons meant that, as I moved to avoid enemies, I would shoot away from the horde, toward nothing. Eventually, I was able to unlock better weapons that would actually hit the enemies approaching me, but the fact that the earliest weapons are some of the worst means it takes a bit too long to find the fun.

By hour 10 with Vampire Survivors, I had found the characters and weapons I enjoyed using the most. They tended to be the ones that would allow me to exponentially increase in power most smoothly and actually felt like I could survive 20+ minutes and 40+ levels into a single run. From that point onwards, Warhammer Survivors is as good as Vampire Survivorsor any other game of its ilk. It’s just not quite as instantly captivating and rewarding.

Diehard Warhammer fans who haven’t played Vampire Survivors or any of the games it inspired will have a fantastic time with this, but there’s not much reason to abandon the original Vampire Survivors for this official clone. Warhammer Survivors certainly won’t usurp its direct inspiration as my go-to game of this style because it forgets to emulate some of what made Vampire Survivors near-perfect. Still, it confidently delivers exactly what the title promises.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

#3582. Chris Pratt Lost Chuck To Zachary Levi. Years Later, Jurassic World Gave Him A Full-Circle Moment

Being a struggling actor in Hollywood is tough, and even huge stars like Chris Pratt go through the wringer early in their careers (like working at Bubba Gump Shrimp). Such was the case when Pratt lost out on the titular role on the show Chuck. Pratt auditioned for the role in 2007, but lost it to Zachary Levi. That has got to be hard enough, but for Pratt, it was made worse as he was taunted by a billboard for the show in LA. Pratt got the last laugh on the casting directors of the show years later when he got his own poster on the same building for Jurassic World.

After trying out for and not making the final cut for Chuck, things got worse when a billboard Pratt could see from his apartment went up advertising the show, with Levi featured on it. Pratt recently talked about it with Barstool:

I did a screen test for Chuck. I wanted it so bad, and then there was this giant billboard across from my apartment of Zach Levi as Chuck, and I’m like, ‘grrr.’

Imagine waking up every morning and looking out the window at a billboard that you hoped would have your face on it, only to see someone else you lost out to. It would be maddening! Pratt kept at it, of course, and eventually landed gigs in Jennifer’s Body and Moneyball, before really breaking big as part of the ensemble cast of Parks and Rec. It wasn’t until 2015 when the moment came full circle, at the premiere of one of Pratt’s earliest blockbusters, Jurassic World.

The moment wasn’t lost on Pratt, as he explained:

Then that same building is where we had the premiere for Jurassic World. And that same building had a giant poster on it with me on a motorcycle, and I was like, 'whoa!'

That really is coming full circle, from what sounds like a real low point early in his career to the triumph of starring in one of the biggest franchises in Hollywood history. Jurassic World came right on the heels of Pratt joining the MCU as Star-Lord in the first Guardians of the Galaxy, so he had become one of the biggest movie stars on the planet.

So does this mean he’s got a “hidden rivalry” with Levi? Well, probably not. He doesn’t seem to have an animosity towards the Shazam! star, just frustration for not getting a part at that point in his career. It’s safe to say that things have worked out pretty well for Pratt, who will next be seen on the 2026 movie schedule in Way of the Warrior Kid, which will be available to watch with an Apple TV subscription.

#3581. George Lucas Expected Star Wars To Be Compared To A Sci-Fi Movie He Says Is Even Better

It's easy to underplay just how monumental "Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope" was at the time of its original theatrical release in 1977. George Lucas' decision to keep the licensing and merchandising rights for the film resulted in a multi-billion-dollar lesson for every studio in Hollywood, while the special effects pioneered by the movie paved the way for the VFX industry we have today. It's also, quite simply, a very good film that combines an eclectic collection of influences to deliver a hugely entertaining space opera with the flair of Westerns and samurai flicks.

Still, while "Star Wars" is typically counted amongst the best sci-fi movies of all time (including by us here at /Film!), Lucas doesn't entirely consider it a sci-fi film. In a 1977 interview with Rolling Stone, he even described the movie as being closer to a Western than, specifically, Stanley Kubrick's classic 1968 sci-fi saga "2001: A Space Odyssey." As Lucas put it:

"I am fairly pleased that they haven't compared it that much to '2001.' Actually, it is being compared more to Westerns than '2001,' which is really what it should be. On a technical level, it can be compared, but personally, I think that '2001' is far superior."

But Lucas wasn't merely being coy about his admiration for Kubrick's movie, he was being practical about the stark differences between the two films. "You know, it had 10 times more money and time, and obviously, it came out better. In special effects, one of the key elements is time and money," he continued. "Most of those special effects in 'Star Wars' were first-time special effects — we shot them, we composited them, and they're in the movie."

It's neither news nor a surprise that George Lucas has always admired Stanley Kubrick's "2001: A Space Odyssey." After all, Lucas originally went to Douglas Trumbull, who had done the visual effects for Kubrick's film, to work on "Star Wars." However, it was only after Trumbull passed on the project that he recommended John Dykstra instead. This resulted in a collaboration that changed the special effects industry forever, as Dykstra pioneered a motion control camera that allowed Lucas to pull off the climactic Death Star trench run in "Star Wars."

But it wasn't just Trumbull that he tried to recruit from the crew behind Kubrick's film. In fact, Lucas' first choice of cinematographer for "Star Wars" was "2001" director of photography Geoffrey Unsworth, who seemed like an ideal pick to capture the documentary feel that Lucas wanted while at the same time being able to handle the movie's visual effects demands. And when Unsworth declined the offer, Lucas ended up going with a different Kubrick cinematographer in the form of Gilbert Taylor (who had worked on "Dr. Strangelove").

Yet again, this creative decision proved essential to making "Star Wars" as unique and effective as it is. Indeed, Taylor managed to ground the movie's operatic spectacle, at times creating a fly-on-the-wall visual sensibility. It makes it seem as though you're not just watching some grand fairy tale set in space but real events that happened a long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away.

#3580. A Sci-Fi Novel Just Won the Booker Prize for the First Time

M. John Harrison's The End of Everything wins the prestigious literary award

M. John Harrison's The End of Everything was awarded the 2026 Booker Prize. This marks the first time that a sci-fi novel has won the prestigious literary award for works of fiction in English published in the United Kingdom or Ireland.

The award marks the capstone of a 60-year career for Harrison, who published his first short story in 1966. The author is widely considered one of the most original voices in British fantasy and sci-fi. Harrison also worked as an editor, reviewer, and critic for New Worlds, a seminal magazine that contributed to the rise of the "New Wave" of science fiction in Britain in the 1970s. Harrison earned many awards over his long career, including both the Arthur C. Clarke Award and the Philip K. Dick Award in 2007 for his novel Nova Swing.

The End of Everything is a post-apocalyptic novel that is as much about an alien catastrophe as it is about the efforts to ignore it. A sequel of sorts to Harrison's 2017 short story, "The Crisis," the book is set on the south coast of England. Protagonist Philip Tennent has moved to the small town of Dalston-on-Sea from London after the capital has been taken over by the ephemeral aliens known as iGhetti. Only that the creatures didn't really "take over" anything; they just fluctuate and evolve, impervious to any attacks. And no one knows if they're actually aliens, either.

Tennent scrapes by collecting alien artifacts from the beach and selling them. One day, something stranger than usual shows up: a baby-like hybrid that keeps growing and learning. But Tennent and his aunt Marnie are only interested in getting rid of it. Around them, a strange apocalypse unfolds. Extreme violence suddenly breaks out and refugees are trying to leave the British Isles to reach mysterious Europe; on the other hand, pensioners and weekenders regularly fill the cafés on the seafront, forsaking any efforts to make sense of what's going on around them.

On his blog, Harrison described The End of Everything as something "that might have been submitted for serialisation in New Worlds in 1967." In fact, the author's body of work cannot be properly assessed without looking at the years he spent at New Worlds, where he built strong professional and personal ties with the most important British science fiction writers of that generation. Chief among them was Michael Moorcock (author of the Elric of Melniboné stories, among many others), to whom Harrison's first novel is dedicated.

The New Wave was a movement that developed in Britain between the late 1960s and the 1970s, before becoming popular in the United States too. The authors associated with the movement applied the rebellious and experimental spirit of their time to a genre that had become extremely popular in the previous decades, but was still associated with a "lower" form of literature. New Wave writers eschewed the "hard sciences" that were the foundation of the work of their illustrious predecessors such as Arthur C. Clarke, Isaac Asimov, and Robert Heinlein. Instead, the New Wave drew from social sciences to step away from the pulp roots of science fiction.

Exploring the foundational classics, international gems, and psychological thrillers that built the modern genre

New Wave writers shaped the modern perception of science fiction, opening the way for further experimentation in the following decades with the Cyberpunk revolution. Harrison can be rightfully counted among the likes of Moorcock, Ursula K. Le Guin, J. G. Ballard, Philip K. Dick, Samuel R. Delany, Roger Zelazny, and Kurt Vonnegut. The feeling of exploring something untold and unfathomable about human existence that recurs in many New Wave works is also strong in The End of Everything, which the author described as a portrayal of "the failure of explanation in society."

M. John Harrison also wrote many books outside the confines of science fiction. The semi-autobiographical novel Climbers stemmed from Harrison's passion for mountain-climbing, while The Course of the Heart is an urban occult fantasy story that had a major influence on the development of the New Weird genre.

#3579. How Wyatt Fits Into Sam's NCIS: New York Team Explained By Shane Harper

LL Cool J’s Sam Hanna has returned to the Big Apple for NCIS: New York, and Shane Harper’s Wyatt Sellers is one of his new Naval Criminal Investigative Service colleagues.

Last month, NCIS: New York premiered on CBS, serving as the long-running procedural franchise’s eighth installment. New York arrives nearly 20 years after LL Cool J first started playing Sam in NCIS: Los Angeles, which ended in 2023 after 14 seasons. The actor then reprised Sam in a recurring capacity on NCIS: Hawai’i, as well as made a handful of guest appearances on the main NCIS.

While Sam initially only came back to New York to investigate the murder of a close friend, he decided to stay and lead a new NCIS team alongside his “roguish partner” Scott Caan’s Nick Schaeffer. This quartet of field agents includes Harper’s Wyatt, who’s usually working alongside Jacqueline Byers’ Addy Ross. Early into season 1, Wyatt has already proven himself to be an integral member of this team that also includes Assistant Special Agent-in-Charge of NCIS’s New York office, Robyn Wells (Jennifer Beals), and Technical Operator Sean Sullivan (Devin Druid).

In an interview with ScreenRant’s Adam Holmes, Harper opened up about Wyatt’s role in NCIS: New York beyond apprehending bad guys. One of the few personal details that’s been revealed about the character so far is that his fiancée broke up with him shortly before the series began, and he’s had no luck selling the engagement ring. Harper shared that New York will explore Wyatt’s former engagement in depth later in the season, though unfortunately for him, that ring isn’t going anywhere:

Coming into these embodying these new characters, we're always looking for little pieces to latch onto because we don't know that much about them. So, as an actor, I'm experiencing what the audience is experiencing as well, where it's like, ‘What's going on? I want to know more about this.’ I'm excited to say that… no spoilers, but we are exploring that, and we have been exploring that more in an intimate way to get more of an understanding of him and this ex-fiancée and all of that. So not giving too much away, but we touch on that and a lot more.

I think that's the fun thing about a show like this: we have 20 episodes to slowly unveil more of the personal stuff, which I think the audiences want. They like the procedural, the ‘what's the new case,’ but then slowly peeling back the layers of the characters is certainly really fun for us as actors, and also I think fun for the audience.

It's funny, and I don't think this will spoil anything too much, but the ring is still around. He hasn't sold it yet. I don't know if he's going to sell it or if he's going to maybe find someone new to give it to, but there hasn't been an episode yet where the ring gets sold. So I have to talk to Byron about that, but it's a really funny bit. At least I thought it was really funny.

As far as Wyatt’s partnership with Addy goes, the latter pokes fun at the former quite often, particularly for his failed attempts to sell the ring, as well as how he likes drinking milk. However, it all comes from a good place, and Addy and Wyatt make an effective investigatory duo. Harper said the following regarding what he likes about their dynamic:

I think there's a real yin yang with them. I think Addy has that New York edge and swagger, and Wyatt, it's the opposite of that. But I like the way that they complement each other. It’s interesting to see them play off of each other and continue to learn about each other. I have to take quite a bit of ribbing from Addy, which is okay. I think as the as the story progresses with them, they'll start to pick up things about each other as the friendship builds, and I don't know if there's going to be more than friendship there. You certainly could see something like that happening.

I don't know if it will, but I really like their relationship and the way that they work together on the cases. They ping pong back and forth, and they feel like a kind of classic duo when they're out on the field. I love when we have to do field days together because we'll be out in the city solving the cases being just the two of us, and I have a good time when we're filming that stuff together.

At the end of the episode “Carousel,” Wyatt and Addy’s relationship entered new territory when she agreed to answer 10 of his personal questions about her. However, at the beginning of the following episode, “Homecoming,” it sounded as though the number had been increased back to 20. Harper described the discrepancy thusly:

That's really funny. So yeah, at the beginning of four, this is really great, but Jackie and I did a bit of ad-libbing at the top of four where we're arguing about how many questions we actually did settle on. I don’t know if we had intentionally done that or if we had read the script and been like, ‘We should add this in,’ but that is in there. If you go back … because the director was like, ‘Do some preamble, and so we were like, ‘Well no, I told you it's 10.’ There was a little bit of that: how many questions do we actually get?

So to be honest, I think maybe they're still unclear, although I'm convinced that it is 10. But they have been going back and forth on it quite a bit. I think the fact that the characters are also in their universe, they're also confused about any questions that they're owed, if that does anything for anyone.

ScreenRant: How’s your experience been working with LL Cool J, the guy on the cast who goes back nearly 20 years with the NCIS franchise?

It's a neat experience … The way that he approaches his work after what he did 14 seasons on NCIS: Los Angeles, so much success both in music and in acting, and for someone that's been as famous for as long as he's been, and to act the way that he does is really remarkable. He's so wonderful to work with, and is such a great leader, and really shines a light on everyone, gives everyone their flowers, and is really encouraging.

When he walks on a set, it's like he's walking onto a new show. He has so much enthusiasm. I don't know how he does that, but it's really great to work with him, and I'm learning a lot from his approach to the creative process and the long hours and the commitment to the job. He's all about the audience. He’s all about [how] we’re making something for people to put on at home and relax and have fun and enjoy being entertained by by a show that hopefully gets the job done. He’s all about the audience and working really hard, which I think we're all falling in line with that because we really appreciate it.

You never know [with] these big stars. You never know how they're going to be. Sometimes they can be difficult, and he's the opposite. So I think we're all just enjoying that process.

ScreenRant: You mentioned in a previous interview that there was about 20 minutes cut from the NCIS: New York pilot, including a scene where you ended up drinking 4–5 glasses of milk. What was some of the other material that was cut?

So just for the fans, the milk scene, there was a really great moment with Addy and Wyatt talking about them being great partners, and there was a moment where they were like, ‘We’re great partners.’ Obviously they're very different, but they have this moment where they’re like, ‘We’re a good team,’ and then Wyatt is still focused on the ring, and he's pretty sad.

It's a moment of sadness, which, again, we don't know what's going to make these final cuts. It's interesting because he is going through this heartbreak. That was a closing scene in the pilot, and he's quite sad, and you get to feel that for him, which I really liked. So that was that piece, and that’s the scene where I was drinking the milk, if you can believe it. It was a very sentimental piece, but at the top of the scene, I'm chugging milk. It’s very funny.

But there was another scene that we did at a halal cart that was really fun, a little bit more conversational stuff with Addy and Wyatt. But there was a lot. Just those two scenes for us are off the top of my head, and then for the rest of the characters, there's a bunch of other stuff. There was a lot of material to work with, but I definitely liked the halal cart scene as well. I didn't eat the halal though, because I was worried that … I don't like talking with my mouth full in the scene, so I was acting like I was about to eat it. But then it worked for my character. I was like, he's such an out-of-towner. He's probably never had halal before, so he didn't even know how to eat it.

It was funny. Yesterday, we were filming another scene. I'm filming a scene, and I asked for oat milk instead of whole milk because I just wanted it to be easier on the tummy.

ScreenRant: What characters from other NCIS shows would you like Wyatt to meet?

I'm not sure. I guess that could be fun for him to maybe meet … I know they were talking about [Sam’s] old partner from Los Angeles coming back, [that] could be fun. Anyone that ties into Sam Hanna's world that can give Wyatt more understanding of Sam would be cool. So anyone that [Sam’s] had any kind of meaningful interactions with either on the field or off, I think could be interesting.

I think the fans too are obviously looking forward to potential crossovers, and I think we're in big support of of that because we're all newbies. Anyone that would get the fans excited, that are fan favorites that could maybe pop over for a few episodes, I think would be good. It just always gets everyone jazzed.

ScreenRant: I’d like to get your thoughts about NCIS: New York’s most important star: Duncan, a.k.a. Sid [the dog].

It's funny because our cinematographer is Sid, and I think that's why they named Duncan Sid. So that's a fun tidbit, he’s named after our DP, which is fun. But Duncan is really great. I grew up with two pit bulls myself, and I have a real soft spot for Duncan. I don't interact with him enough, even though Wyatt's definitely an animal person. So I would like to get some more cuddles … Addy’s always playing with the dog at the top of a scene or something, but it’s never me. So I feel like they need to change that because I'm a dog guy. I love dogs, and particularly pit bulls.

But it's funny, because I think there was a post yesterday that went up with Jennifer and Duncan walking around. I don't know if you saw that, it was a BTS video, and it got so many views. Dog videos just get so many views. Everyone loves them. [Duncan's] the star. I just told Jennifer Beals yesterday, the fans are going crazy for her and Duncan. But yeah, Duncan's great, and Sid is a very important character that hopefully will be featured many, many, many more times in the future.

He's so good. He's so well-behaved and so sweet, and he'll just come up to you on a break and just give you a little snuggle, and then go back to his mark. It's wild. He's a very good performer. The other funny thing that we do is there's a big stuffed animal that we'll use when he's not ready to come to set yet. I don't know where he is. I don't know if he's in the hair and makeup chair or something, but Jackie will be rehearsing with this giant stuffed animal, and I get a kick out of that. I think it's really funny.

ScreenRant: What was it that drew you to working on NCIS: New York when you first read the pilot script?

Well, I thought the pilot was incredibly fun and action-packed. [It had] all of the pieces of a great pilot. It was paced really well. The characters were extremely well-defined, and it was just a really perfect pilot. And then when I heard that Byron Belasco was doing it, and he was going to be the showrunner and executive producer. I was really excited about that because I'm a big fan of his, and I really loved Kingdom and the other things that he's worked on.

So that drew me to it. And I'd never done a network show like this in the capacity that I'm doing, and I, to be honest, have always wanted to be a part of a big network show like this. So when I initially read for this, it's one actor in a million. There are difficult roles to get, so I wasn't expecting it to even go my way, but I obviously had my fingers crossed, and here we are.

ScreenRant: How has working on NCIS: New York compared to your time on Power Book IV?

It's different. It's funny, I’ve joked around when people stop me, and they know me from Power, and then they will talk to me about NCIS. The bit that we have is, I'm going from playing a gangster to playing a badge, or a shield as we say, in New York. It's interesting to be on the other side of the law there, and I'm honestly still adjusting to playing like a very wholesome character. I'm still figuring it out.

We're halfway through right now. I'm starting episode 11 tonight. I'm gonna leave for set in a few hours, but it's still an adjustment because that role in Power was, like everything in Power is, so hard edged. I loved the crew and the cast and the producers on Power. I love everyone on this show, and we do also get a lot of that good New York grit in NCIS as well that I know [LL Cool J] certainly is interested in finding all the things that we love about the NCIS world, and also servicing more of a New York edge and flair to it, which has been really fun as well. Two very different projects, but I'm enjoying them equally.

ScreenRant: What’s been your favorite location to film in for NCIS: New York so far?

Well, it's hard to beat Central Park, which was in the pilot. Central Park was pretty extraordinary to be in with a big film crew. That was pretty awesome. Again, the Diamond District was really cool as well. Also, in the pilot, we filmed right here in Williamsburg, near the docks, where [there’s] the beautiful view of the city. I think it’s in Episode 2, there’s a car crash scene down there that we filmed. It's an empty lot, and you get the whole skyline looking over the river. That location's been really fun. We’ve been there a couple times because it's so nice and it looks good. I like it down there a lot.

I'm trying to think if there are any other interesting locations. We're all over the city. We're all over Brooklyn. I think it's a big part of the fun. It’s just getting to be out there amongst it. And the New Yorkers have been nice so far, so hopefully we don't overstay our welcome when we're parking our big trailers out in a city that already doesn't have parking. There's a lot of stuff filming in the city I think is really good for the entertainment community and everything. So yeah, we're happy to be here.

NCIS: New York airs Tuesdays at 9 p.m. ET on CBS's fall 2026 schedule.

#3578. How To Watch Brad Pitt's Heart Of The Beast At Home

David Ayer's "Heart of the Beast" wasn't really a sleeper hit, given that it stars Brad Pitt, but the harrowing survival film turned out to be a surprisingly leggy box office performer thanks to solid word of mouth. Now it's about to find a wider audience as it moves to streaming on November 10 (as the opening of Pitt's kinda-sorta anticipated "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" nears).

The film caught on with moviegoers due to its deeply affecting narrative about a retired Army veteran (Pitt) and his combat dog struggling to survive in the Alaskan wilderness after their seaplane crashes. The crash is caused by Pitt's character having a heart attack, but he's not down for the count — not yet. He and his dog are uniquely equipped to hoof it 58 miles back to civilization, but this terrain is every bit as treacherous as a battle zone. Along the way, they encounter wolves (dredging up memories of Joe Carnahan's "The Grey"), a grizzly bear and other obstacles that test their resolve. Each challenge leaves them a little (or a lot) worse for the wear, but they are determined to emerge from this ordeal as they've done so often in their war-torn past.

Again, "Heart of the Beast" will begin streaming via Premium VOD on November 10, and consumers will get a few extras to go along with their purchase.

According to a press release issued by Paramount today, the PVOD "Heart of the Beast" will include a behind-the-scenes featurette titled "One Last Mission," which is said to be a "love letter to the land, the people, and most of all the dogs who made this film shine." (Their names are Uber, Seeka and Ryker.) Because you can never get enough good-dog footage, there's also "Uber & Brad: A Soulful Bond." Not sure why Seeka and Ryker were denied a mention here, but I guess I'll find out when I watch it. Finally, there are deleted scenes that promise to "play tug of war with your heart strings," so get ready to weep some more once you've finished the film (and you will weep).

While it would've been nice if this visually stunning film remained in theaters for a little while longer, it was clear from jump that its destiny was to become a dad movie classic. It'll be streaming for years and years to come, forcing grown men to complain about their dusty living rooms/man caves. And if you're one of those people who needs to know the fate of the pooch ahead of time, /Film's got you covered.

#3577. Christopher Nolan's Batman Begins Borrowed Part Of Its Plot From A Beloved Animated Series Episode

In each of the three "Dark Knight" trilogy films, the villains make an attempt to destroy Gotham City from within. In "Batman Begins," one of those villains is Doctor Jonathan Crane/The Scarecrow (Cillian Murphy). The head of Gotham's Arkham Asylum, Crane is obsessed with fear. With ingredients provided by the League of Shadows, he's manufactured a "fear toxin" that can drive anyone exposed to it to terror. Using Arkham inmates, Crane has been dumping the toxin into Gotham's water supply via the asylum's pipe systems.

"Scarecrow tries to infect Gotham City with fear toxin" has become a stock "Batman" plot, like in the 2015 video game "Batman: Arkham Knight" or the 2021 comic crossover "Fear State." Look back, though, and you'll find it before "Batman Begins" — specifically, in "Batman: The Animated Series" episode "Dreams in Darkness," written by Judith and Garfield Reeves-Stevens. Batman, exposed to the Scarecrow's fear toxin and suffering hallucinations, is judged insane and locked inside Arkham as a patient.

Under his doctors' noses, Scarecrow plots to dump his toxin into an underground river that flows into Gotham's reservoirs, infecting the city and sparking a mass frenzy of fear. Crane isn't doing it for ransom or a statement; a former academic, he's running a mass experiment in studying the psychological effects of fear.

Still, it's hard to write off the similarities between "Dreams in Darkness" and "Batman Begins" as coincidental. The scene of Batman (Christian Bale) defeating Crane is even taken from a different "Batman: The Animated Series" episode: Scarecrow's debut, "Nothing to Fear." Batman poisons Scarecrow with "his own medicine," causing Crane to hallucinate Batman as not merely a man in a bat costume but a demonic, man-sized bat creature.

Whereas in "Dreams in Darkness" Crane is moving in and out of his cell, "Batman Begins" put him in control of Arkham (reimagining Crane's original backstory as a college professor). "Dark Knight" trilogy co-writer David S. Goyer has said he convinced Christopher Nolan that Scarecrow needed to wear his mask, and they devised a practical reason: The mask is a gas mask that keeps Crane from ingesting his fear toxin and scaring his victims who do. That is not the case in "Dreams in Darkness," where Crane is exposed to the toxin while in costume and ends the episode back in his cell as a hysterical mess.

Goyer has said the selection of Scarecrow as the villain of "Batman Begins" came out of the movie's theme of confronting fear. If you're going to steal, steal from the best, because "Dreams in Darkness" is a masterclass at showing Scarecrow getting under Batman's skin. It's the most frightening Scarecrow episode of "Batman: The Animated Series" and the only one that actually comes close to being a horror story, thanks to Batman's repeated and menacing hallucinations.

The first fright is a jump scare; Batman sees the Joker walking towards him reflected on the Batcomputer's screen, only to turn around and find it was Alfred. The terror doesn't let up, and once Batman makes it to Arkham, there's also the dash of psychological horror. Batman is locked in the same asylum as his greatest foes, where no one believes his pleas, and their doubt could cost a city's worth of lives. Granted, the doctors' refusal to believe Batman does border on incompetence. Scarecrow wanting to poison the city is just another night in Gotham, but Arkham's staff treat Batman like he's raving mad.

Many of the best "Batman: The Animated Series" episodes feel like 22-minute film noirs, and "Dreams in Darkness" is no exception. The episode begins in media res at Arkham, with the opening twist that the "new patient" the doctors are talking about is Batman. Batman gets a voiceover narration — a noir staple — as flashbacks explain how he ended up in a straitjacket.

The hallucinations get worse before they get better. Batman's cell door swings wide open, bathing him in a hellish red light. His parents walk into a dark tunnel, disappearing as that tunnel becomes the barrel of a giant handgun. Once Batman escapes and makes it to the caverns where Scarecrow dwells, he imagines a rat taking on the Joker's face. Imagined villains then keep gruesomely metamorphosing into others. As Batman imagines himself falling into an abyss, the darkness becomes a spiral shape with Scarecrow's face in the center.

It's beautifully animated and genuinely creepy stuff; the central image of Batman falling looks right out of Alfred Hitchcock's "Vertigo."

As for the straw-man of the hour, Scarecrow doesn't appear much. He only shows up onscreen halfway through and spends his time waiting on a countdown for his experiment. But "Dreams in Darkness" is Scarecrow voice actor Henry Polic II's best, and most subtle, performance in the role. His baritone is soft, almost mellifluous, which only makes moments like Scarecrow's cruel snicker at how he's left Batman "much, much worse" off than death more unnerving. Polic's time as Scarecrow can be overshadowed by Jeffrey Combs' later, superior performance on "The New Batman Adventures," but "Dreams in Darkness" shows he could be as great a Scarecrow as Combs — or, indeed, Cillian Murphy.
